**Allegheny County** was formed in 1788 from Westmoreland and Washington Counties. Pittsburgh was incorporated as a city in 1816 and sits at the confluence of the Allegheny, Monongahela, and Ohio rivers. The county held authority over court, deed, probate, and (from 1885) marriage registration throughout the target period.

**Critical quirk — Allegheny City (pre-1907):** The city of Allegheny (now Pittsburgh's North Side) was a separate municipality within Allegheny County until it was annexed by Pittsburgh in 1907. Families living north of the Allegheny River before 1907 generated records under *Allegheny City*, not Pittsburgh proper. Search both city record sets.

Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide registration of births or deaths until **1906** (state level). For the 1865–1905 window you are researching, vital events were recorded inconsistently at the local/church level. There was no statewide death registration before 1906, and no statewide birth registration in effect during the steel boom decades. Church records and local Pittsburgh Board of Health filings are the primary substitutes.

---

## 2. FamilySearch Collections (Pennsylvania Level)

The following collections are available on FamilySearch for Pennsylvania and overlap the target period. *(Volume-level digitization data is unavailable in this environment — access levels below are derived from collection metadata only.)*

| Collection | ID | Date Range | Records | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages | 1921317 | 1885–1950 | 524,189 | Begins mid-target period; covers Allegheny County marriage records |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages | 1571957 | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | Broader compilation; overlaps entire period |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages | 1502909 | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | Compiled abstracts; no images |
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records | 1999196 | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | Covers wills, inventories, administration — useful for estates of workers |
| Pennsylvania, Death Certificates | 2255317 | **1906–1968** | 4,218,763 | Starts just *after* the core period; captures deaths of people who worked in the boom era |

🔎 FamilySearch: [https://www.familysearch.org/search/](https://www.familysearch.org/search/)

---

## 3. Vital Records

**State-level registration:** Statewide birth and death registration began in Pennsylvania at the **state level** in **1906** only. The FamilySearch wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records did not resolve to specific content — consult the article directly at `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records` for local-level dates.

**What to use instead for 1865–1905:**
- **Pittsburgh Board of Health death registers** — Pittsburgh maintained its own local death records before statewide registration. These are held at the **Pittsburgh City Archives** and partially at the **Allegheny County Health Department**. They may capture cause of death, occupation, and birthplace.
- **Church registers** — See §6 below. Baptism (birth substitute), marriage, and burial records from ethnic parishes are the primary vital-event source for this period.
- **Marriage records:** Pennsylvania County Marriages (1885–1950, FamilySearch collection 1921317) begins in 1885 and is the most accessible source for Allegheny County marriages in the late boom period.

---

## 4. Census Records

Federal censuses are the backbone of working-class research in this period. The **occupation column** is especially rich for tracing steel workers across census years.

| Census Year | Coverage | Key Occupational Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **1870** | ✅ Full | Occupation, real estate value, personal estate |
| **1880** | ✅ Full | Occupation, relationship to head, birthplace of parents |
| **1890** | ⚠️ **Largely destroyed** | Fire in 1921 destroyed most schedules — a significant gap for Pittsburgh families at the height of the boom |
| **1900** | ✅ Full | Occupation, years in U.S., citizenship status — critical for immigrant steel workers |

**Substitute for 1890 loss:** City directories (see §8), state records, and church registers for 1888–1895 fill this gap. The **1890 Veterans' Schedule** (Union veterans) survived and is on FamilySearch — relevant for Civil War–era workers now in the mills.

**Mortality Schedules (1850–1885):** These census supplements recorded deaths in the year preceding the enumeration and note occupation and cause of death — valuable for identifying workers who died on or near the job.

---

## 5. Church Records *(Critical for this period)*

Because civil registration was absent or unreliable before 1906, ethnic parish registers are often the *only* source for births, marriages, and deaths of immigrant steel workers. Pittsburgh's boom drew massive waves from specific regions; parishes organized ethnically:

| Ethnic Group | Denomination | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Irish | Roman Catholic | St. Patrick's (Downtown), St. Brigid's |
| German | Roman Catholic / Lutheran | Numerous German national parishes; German Lutheran congregations |
| Polish | Roman Catholic | St. Stanislaus Kostka parish (South Side) — one of the first Polish parishes in the U.S. |
| Slovak | Roman Catholic / Lutheran | Immaculate Heart of Mary (Southside Slopes) — first Slovak Catholic parish in the U.S. |
| Croatian | Roman Catholic | St. Nicholas Croatian (South Side) |
| Italian | Roman Catholic | St. Peter of Alcantara, Bloomfield |
| African American | Methodist / Baptist | Wesley Center AME Zion; Mt. Ararat Baptist |

**Where records are held:**
- Parish registers remain with individual parishes or have been transferred to the **Pittsburgh Catholic Diocese Archives** (Diocese of Pittsburgh).
- Many German Lutheran registers are at the **Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA) Region 8 Archives** or were microfilmed by the Genealogical Society of Utah (LDS) — check FamilySearch catalog.
- The FamilySearch wiki_search result confirms Catholic parishes served specific ethnic communities and their registers are often the best source for family data.

**Digitization level:** Mostly **physical/microfilm only** for Allegheny County church records in this period. Check the FamilySearch catalog for individual parish microfilm holdings before making an in-person visit.

---

## 6. Industrial & Occupational Records *(Primary Focus)*

This is the richest and most distinctive record category for late 1800s Pittsburgh research. These records do not replace vital or census records but can uniquely document an ancestor's work history, employer, wages, and union affiliation.

### a) Company Employment Records
Steel company employment records for this era are **fragmentary** — most were not retained by the companies and did not pass to government custody. What survives:

- **Heinz History Center** (Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh) — the premier repository for Pittsburgh industrial and immigration records. Holds surviving employment ledgers, company histories, and labor records from Carnegie Steel and successor firms. Contact: `https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org/`
- **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area Archives** — focuses on the steel corridor along the Monongahela River (Homestead, Braddock, Duquesne). Holds records related to U.S. Steel and Carnegie Steel's Homestead Works. Contact: `https://www.riversofsteel.com/`
- **Homestead Strike of 1892 records** — the 1892 Carnegie/Homestead lockout generated newspaper coverage, legal records, and congressional testimony that names individual workers. Pennsylvania State Archives and the Library of Congress hold related materials.

### b) Union Records
- **Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers** — the primary union for the Pittsburgh steel trades in this era. Membership rolls and meeting minutes survive at the **Historical Collections and Labor Archives, Penn State University (University Park)**: `https://libraries.psu.edu/hcla`
- Union records may list member name, lodge number, residence, occupation, and date joined.

### c) State Factory Inspection Reports
Pennsylvania established a Bureau of Factory Inspection in **1889**. Annual reports were published by the state and list inspected factories by name, location, number of employees (sometimes by nationality), and violations. These are not individual employee records, but they document which mills were active and their workforce composition.
- Held at: **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg; also partially available in digitized state documents collections.

### d) City Directories *(Occupational substitute)*
Pittsburgh city directories list residents by name with **occupation and employer** and are published annually. The **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds a nearly complete run from the **1810s** onward — this is an unbroken run through the entire steel boom period.
- Useful for tracking a worker year-by-year, identifying boarders in steel-worker households, and locating mill towns.
- Directories also have **reverse (street) listings** — useful for identifying neighbors and co-workers.
- Partially digitized on **Ancestry.com** (U.S. City Directories, 1822–1995) and **Fold3**.

### e) Federal Census Occupation Columns
As noted in §4, the 1870, 1880, and 1900 census schedules all include occupation. The 1880 census also includes a **Manufacturers' Schedule** (not yet widely indexed) that records establishment-level data for mills and factories in Allegheny County — useful for locating an ancestor's workplace.

---

## 7. Immigration & Naturalization

The steel boom's workforce was overwhelmingly immigrant. Naturalization records are essential and often contain more biographical detail than any other source.

**Before 1906:** Naturalization could occur in *any* court of record. For Allegheny County, primary courts were:
- **Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas** — holds declaration of intent ("first papers") and petitions for naturalization. Records are held at the **Allegheny County Courthouse** and have been partially microfilmed.
- The FamilySearch wiki confirms naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse as a key source.

**After 1906:** Naturalization was centralized through the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization. Records are at the **National Archives at Philadelphia** (NARA Mid-Atlantic Region): `https://www.archives.gov/philadelphia`

**Passenger lists:** NARA holds passenger manifests for the port of entry (most immigrants arrived via New York/Ellis Island or Baltimore). FamilySearch and Ancestry have indexed passenger lists for this period. Manifests from c. 1895 onward include the destination (often naming a Pittsburgh-area contact or employer).

---

## 8. Newspapers

Pittsburgh newspapers of the period documented mill accidents, strikes, union elections, obituaries, and community news in ethnic neighborhoods:

- **Pittsburgh Post-Gazette** (established 1786) — major daily; extensive coverage of Carnegie Steel and the 1892 Homestead Strike
- **Pittsburgh Dispatch** (1846–1923) — second major daily
- **Ethnic-language papers** (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, German) — often name individuals not found in English-language papers

Access:
- **Newspapers.com** and **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free): `https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/`
- The **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds microfilm runs of local papers.

---

## 9. Probate, Land & Court Records

- **Probate:** Pennsylvania Probate Records (FamilySearch collection 1999196, 1683–1994, 893,214 records) covers Allegheny County. Wills of mill workers often list tools, boarding arrangements, and family members still in the home country.
- **Deed records:** Allegheny County deed books at the **Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds**. Working-class families in Pittsburgh often rented, but property purchases and tax records identify neighborhood of residence.
- **Court records:** The Court of Common Pleas handled naturalizations, name changes, guardianship, and civil suits (including workplace injury claims, especially post-1890s).

---

## 10. Military Records

Many steel workers were Civil War veterans (the 1870–1880 cohort). Pennsylvania Civil War records include:
- **NARA pension files** (RG 15) — often contain family data, maiden names, children's names, and post-war residence
- **Pennsylvania Veterans' Card File** — at the Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Grand Army of the Republic (GAR) post records** — Allegheny County had numerous posts; records may be at the **Heinz History Center** or local historical societies

---

## 11. Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Heinz History Center**, Pittsburgh | Industrial records, immigration records, city directories, newspapers, company histories | In-person; some digitized: heinzhistorycenter.org |
| **Rivers of Steel Archives** | Homestead/Mon Valley mill and labor records | Contact: riversofsteel.com |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories (1810s–), local history, newspapers | In-person; some digitized |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Naturalization, deeds, probate, court records | In-person |
| **Penn State HCLA** (University Park) | Union records (Amalgamated Association) | In-person; finding aids online |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Factory inspection reports, state vital records (post-1906), PA veterans | In-person; some digitized: phmc.pa.gov |
| **NARA Mid-Atlantic** (Philadelphia) | Post-1906 naturalization, federal records | In-person; some digitized: archives.gov |
| **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** | Catholic parish registers | By appointment |
| **FamilySearch** (online) | PA marriages, probate, compiled records | Free: familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** (online) | Census, city directories, passenger lists, newspapers | Subscription |

---

## 12. Adjoining Jurisdictions

The wiki_read for the Allegheny County Genealogy page returned generic content rather than the county's neighboring-counties table, so the adjacent counties are noted here from standard Pennsylvania geographic knowledge but could not be confirmed from a tool result. Families living near county borders — especially in mill towns along the rivers — may have generated records in neighboring counties:

- **Beaver County** (west) — Ambridge, Aliquippa, and other mill towns
- **Washington County** (south) — Monongahela River corridor
- **Westmoreland County** (east/southeast) — Connellsville coke region, which supplied fuel to Pittsburgh furnaces
- **Butler County** (north)
- **Armstrong County** (northeast)

Workers in the **coke and coal region** of Westmoreland and Fayette Counties were directly tied to Pittsburgh's steel supply chain — if your ancestor worked in coke, extend your search to those counties.

---

## 13. Research Quirks & Key Warnings

1. **Allegheny City (pre-1907):** Families north of the Allegheny River before 1907 were in *Allegheny City*, a separate municipality. Check Allegheny City directories and Allegheny City Board of Health records separately from Pittsburgh records.
2. **1890 census largely destroyed:** Use city directories, church records, and factory inspection reports to bridge 1880–1900.
3. **No statewide birth/death registration before 1906:** Church registers and Pittsburgh Board of Health local records are the primary substitutes.
4. **Company employment records are fragmentary:** Do not expect a complete employment file — layer city directories, union records, and census occupation columns to reconstruct a work history.
5. **Ethnic parishes are essential:** Most immigrant steel workers were recorded almost exclusively in their ethnic parish registers. Identify the nationality first, then the likely parish.
6. **Naturalizations pre-1906 were filed in any court:** Check both the Court of Common Pleas and the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania (NARA Philadelphia).
7. **Coke region tie-in:** If your ancestor worked in Pittsburgh steel, check Westmoreland and Fayette County records for relatives who worked in the coal and coke supply chain.
8. **FamilySearch Pennsylvania wiki pages** returned generic fallback content in this session — consult them directly at `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy` and `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy` for current coverage detail.

---

## 14. Digitization Summary

| Record Type | Digitization Level |
|---|---|
| Federal census (1870, 1880, 1900) | **Indexed + images** (FamilySearch, Ancestry) |
| PA County Marriages 1885–1950 | **Indexed + images** (FamilySearch collection 1921317) |
| PA Probate Records 1683–1994 | **Indexed + images** (FamilySearch collection 1999196) |
| PA Death Certificates (from 1906) | **Indexed + images** (FamilySearch collection 2255317) |
| City directories | **Partially indexed** (Ancestry); **browse-only** at Carnegie Library |
| Church registers | Mostly **physical/microfilm only** — check FamilySearch catalog by parish |
| Naturalization records (pre-1906) | **Partially microfilmed** — some indexed, some browse-only at NARA Philadelphia |
| Company employment records | **Physical only**, fragmentary — Heinz History Center, Rivers of Steel |
| Union records (HCLA Penn State) | **Physical only** |
| Factory inspection reports | **Physical only** at PA State Archives |
| Newspapers | **Partially digitized** (Newspapers.com, Chronicling America) |

---

**Where to start:** For most Pittsburgh steel-era families, the recommended sequence is: (1) federal census 1880 + 1900 to establish household and occupation; (2) city directories to track year-by-year; (3) ethnic parish registers for vital events; (4) naturalization records at the Allegheny County Courthouse or NARA Philadelphia; (5) Heinz History Center for any surviving industrial records. The 1892 Homestead Strike records are also worth checking if your ancestor worked at the Homestead Works specifically.

# Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — Locality Guide
## 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic Research

**Jurisdiction:** Philadelphia County / Philadelphia City, Pennsylvania, United States
**Period of interest:** 1793 (epidemic, August–November)
**Guide produced:** 2026-09-08

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Philadelphia County was established in 1682. In 1793, the city of Philadelphia was the capital of the United States, with a population of approximately 50,000 residents. The yellow fever epidemic struck from August through November 1793, killing approximately 5,000 people — roughly one-tenth of the population — while thousands more fled the city. ([Wikipedia, Yellow fever epidemic of 1793](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793))

**Critical boundary note for 1793:** The city of Philadelphia occupied a much smaller footprint than Philadelphia County. Many residents lived in surrounding townships — Northern Liberties, Southwark, Kensington, and others — legally within the county but outside the city proper, with their own separate records. The Consolidation Act of 1854 merged city and county. For 1793 research, always determine whether your ancestor lived in the city or an outlying township before deciding which record series to search.

**Vital registration:** Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration of births, deaths, or marriages in 1793.** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)), statewide registration began in 1906. For 1793, **church records are the only substitute for vital records.**

> **Coverage gap:** The `wiki_place_page` tool returned only generic content for all four Pennsylvania sections (home, getting\_started, online\_records, research\_tips), and `wiki_read` fetches for the Pennsylvania Vital Records and Philadelphia County Genealogy pages also resolved to generic content. Consult [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia\_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy) directly for current collection-level guidance.

---

## Epidemic-Specific Sources ⭐ Start Here

These sources are unique to the 1793 outbreak and are your highest-priority starting points. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)):

### 1. Mathew Carey's Published List of the Dead
*A Short Account of the Malignant Fever Lately Prevalent in Philadelphia* (1793) includes named lists of those who died. Multiple editions exist — later editions are more complete. Search all spelling variants of the surname. Digitized copies are available through HathiTrust. **This is the single fastest way to confirm whether an ancestor died in the epidemic.**

### 2. Committee Minutes and Reports
The "Committee appointed by the citizens" managed relief efforts throughout the epidemic. Their minutes and reports record names of those who received aid and who died. Manuscript sources held at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** and the **Philadelphia City Archives**.

### 3. Bush Hill Hospital Records
Bush Hill served as the city's emergency epidemic hospital. Some records survive and are held at HSP and the Philadelphia City Archives. May document patients admitted, treated, and those who died there.

### 4. Philadelphia Board of Health Records
The Board of Health tracked epidemic deaths. Records held at the **Philadelphia City Archives**.

---

## Church Records (Primary Vital Record Substitute for 1793)

Church burial registers are the most direct genealogical source for epidemic deaths. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)):

- Key churches with surviving records include **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal) and **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church)**, both explicitly named in the Wiki as holding relevant burial records.
- The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records.
- HSP holds transcriptions and microfilm of numerous church registers.
- FamilySearch has microfilmed many Philadelphia church records.

> ⚠️ One collection appearing in the FamilySearch system — *Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records* (ID: SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708–1985) — is **flagged in the tool data as a "synthetic test fixture."** Do not rely on it; verify any Philadelphia church record holdings directly at [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org).

---

## FamilySearch Digital Collections Overlapping 1793

Three indexed FamilySearch collections directly cover the target period:

| Collection | Date Range | ID | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records | 1683–1994 | [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) | Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages | 1677–1950 | [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages | 1700–1900 | [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | Indexed, no images |

**Collections outside the 1793 window** (not applicable for epidemic deaths/marriages, but useful for tracing descendants): Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906–1968 ([2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317)); Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1885–1950 ([1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317)).

> **Gap:** The `volume_search` tool is unavailable in this environment. Browse-only digitized image volumes may exist beyond these indexed collections. Check the FamilySearch Catalog directly for Philadelphia County microfilm and image volumes.

---

## Census Records

| Census | Value for 1793 Epidemic Research |
|---|---|
| **1790 U.S. Federal Census** | Taken 3 years before the epidemic — establishes household composition before the outbreak |
| **1800 U.S. Federal Census** | Taken 7 years after — compare with 1790: members present in 1790 but absent in 1800 may have died in the epidemic or fled permanently |

Both are available on [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch (free).

---

## Probate Records

The epidemic produced a **surge in wills and estate administrations in Philadelphia County in 1793–1795.** This makes probate records an unusually rich source for this period — wills name heirs, executors, creditors, and often describe real and personal property.

- **FamilySearch:** Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 ([collection 1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)) — indexed + images
- **Philadelphia Register of Wills** (Philadelphia City Archives) — original documents, some not yet fully digitized

Search specifically for will dates and letters of administration recorded between August 1793 and mid-1794.

---

## Newspapers

Philadelphia's newspapers published death notices and weekly bills of mortality throughout the epidemic (August–November 1793). A disappeared or newly appearing name across pre- and post-epidemic newspaper runs can be diagnostic.

| Resource | Access |
|---|---|
| [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) | Subscription; searchable digitized newspapers |
| **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress) | Free at chroniclingamerica.loc.gov |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** | Most complete Philadelphia newspaper collection for this period; in-person |

---

## Land, Tax, and City Directory Records

- **Philadelphia city tax records (1790s):** Track residents' presence and property year by year. Held at the Philadelphia City Archives and Pennsylvania State Archives. Disappearance from tax rolls in 1793–1794 may indicate death.
- **Philadelphia city directories (1790s):** Published annually, listing heads of household by address and occupation. A name absent from post-1793 editions but present before is significant. HSP holds a nearly complete run.
- **Land/deed records:** Philadelphia County deeds held at the Philadelphia City Archives; partially indexed on FamilySearch.

---

## Military Records

Many Philadelphia residents in 1793 were Revolutionary War veterans. Pension files often document family composition in detail.

- **Revolutionary War pension files:** NARA; available on [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) and Ancestry
- **Pennsylvania State Archives:** State-level military records

---

## Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | Board of Health, Committee records, tax records, deeds, Register of Wills | In-person; some online |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Manuscripts, church records, newspapers, city directories, Mathew Carey materials | In-person; some digitized |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** | Church record indexes, compiled genealogies | Members; some at HSP |
| **American Philosophical Society** | Benjamin Rush papers, epidemic manuscripts | In-person |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** | Tax assessment rolls, state records | In-person; some online |
| **NARA (Mid-Atlantic Region)** | Federal census, military/pension records | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) |
| **FamilySearch** | Microfilmed church records, probate, marriages | Free; familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census, many Philadelphia church records, city directories | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery records | Free; [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) |

---

## Suggested Research Sequence

1. **Check Mathew Carey's published list** for the surname (all spelling variants).
2. **Search church burial registers** — especially Christ Church and Gloria Dei; also identify your ancestor's denomination and target that church's archive.
3. **Compare the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses** household by household.
4. **Search Philadelphia County probate records** (FamilySearch [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)) for wills and administrations filed 1793–1795.
5. **Search Philadelphia newspapers** from August–November 1793 for death notices and bills of mortality.
6. **Contact HSP and Philadelphia City Archives** for Committee minutes, Board of Health records, and Bush Hill hospital records.
7. **Search Philadelphia city tax records and directories** from before and after 1793 to detect disappearances.

---

## Key Quirks and Cautions

- **No Pennsylvania statewide civil registration in 1793.** Statewide registration began in 1906. Church records are the only vital record substitute — there is no official death register to find.
- **City vs. county boundaries are critical.** In 1793, "Philadelphia" records may cover only the city proper, not the surrounding townships (Northern Liberties, Southwark, etc.). Search at both levels.
- **Mass flight from the city.** Thousands relocated to **Chester, Delaware, Montgomery, and Bucks Counties** during and after the epidemic and never returned. If an ancestor vanishes from Philadelphia records after 1793, search those neighboring counties through at least 1800.
- **Probate windfall.** The epidemic death surge makes Philadelphia County Orphans' Court proceedings from 1793–1795 exceptionally rich — a disproportionate fraction of the city's population filed or had estates administered in that window.
- **Neighboring counties not confirmed by tool:** The Philadelphia County Genealogy wiki page did not return a neighboring-counties table in tool output. Confirm adjacencies directly at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia\_County,\_Pennsylvania\_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy).

# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (ca. 1855–1900, focus on the Great Fire of 1871)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **County formed:** Cook County, 1831
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** No data returned by the place_population tool for this standardPlace.
- **Economy:** Commerce, meatpacking, grain trade, railroads, manufacturing; Chicago was the primary Midwest rail hub by the 1860s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Heavy waves of Irish, German, Scandinavian, and Eastern European immigrants throughout the 1850s–1890s; ethnic enclaves maintained separate churches and foreign-language records.
- **Key historical events:** **Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871** — destroyed ~3.3 square miles, killed ~300 people, left 100,000+ homeless, and wiped out the Cook County Courthouse along with most pre-fire civil records. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire))

## Boundary changes
- Cook County was formed in 1831; its boundaries were stable through the entire target period.

---

## ⚠️ Critical context: The Great Fire and record loss

The fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, which housed **deeds, birth and death registers, court records (probate, naturalization, civil suits), and tax rolls**. The loss is total for most pre-fire county-level civil records. Federal census schedules survived because originals were held in Washington. The **Burnt Record Act of 1872** required property owners to re-register their deeds, creating a partial reconstruction of pre-fire land ownership. **Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records** — now at the Chicago History Museum — became a vital substitute for pre-fire property documentation. City directories from the 1840s onward also survived and are at the Newberry Library.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire); Wikipedia, [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire))*

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date on FamilySearch:** 1871 — the fire destroyed all earlier county registers. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Illinois Vital Records returned only generic fallback content; a specific statewide civil registration start date is not confirmed by tool results.
- **What exists on FamilySearch — all indexed + images:**

| Collection | Records | FamilySearch ID | Dates |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cook County Birth Certificates | 1,450,000 | 2024189 | 1871–1940 |
| Cook County Death Records | 980,000 | 1913456 | 1871–1947 |
| Cook County Marriage Records | 620,000 | 1756321 | 1871–1920 |

- **Pre-fire alternative:** Church registers (below); city directories at the Newberry Library.
- **Where held (originals):** Cook County Clerk's Office (vital records from 1871 onward).

### Church records
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925* — **285,000 records** (collection ID: 1803978) — **indexed + images.** This is the primary pre-fire resource, predating the Courthouse loss by nearly four decades.
- **Catholic records:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's **Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** holds Catholic parish registers. Parish registers that survived the fire or were reconstructed by parishes are the best substitute for missing pre-fire civil vital records.
- **Where held (physical):** Archdiocese of Chicago Bernardin Archives; individual parish offices.
- **Language:** Primarily English; some German and Polish registers for immigrant congregations.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Schedules survive for Cook County/Chicago in 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900. The 1890 census was nationally destroyed. **The 1870 Chicago enumeration is the single most important pre-fire source** — it captures the entire pre-fire population and survived because originals were retained in Washington, not the Courthouse. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))*
- **Access:** 1850–1880 and 1900 are indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry. 1890 is nationally destroyed.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available 1850–1880; list deaths in the year preceding enumeration. The 1880 mortality schedule may capture fire-era victims.

### Probate and court records
- **Pre-fire status:** Probate files, court records, and naturalizations held at the Cook County Courthouse were destroyed in 1871 — a total loss for pre-fire probate.
- **Digitized volumes on FamilySearch** (volume_search returned **totalResults: 2 — complete set**):

| Volume | Record type | Dates | Images | Indexed? | Access level |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 009982110 | Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies) | 1865–1871 | 38 | 0% — not full-text | **Browse-only images** |
| 009982111 | Post-fire Property Re-recordings | 1871–1880 | 112 | 41% — not full-text | **Partially indexed images** |

- **Post-fire records:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University holds Cook County records from 1871 onward.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Illinois is a federal (public) land state — rectangular survey system.
- **Pre-fire disaster:** County deed books in the Courthouse were destroyed in 1871. The **Burnt Record Act of 1872** required re-registration; look for post-1872 deeds citing the original pre-fire instrument. Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records serve as substitute evidence of pre-fire ownership. *(Wikipedia, [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire))*
- **Federal land patents (original grants):** Available at the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) — held federally, not in the Courthouse, and survived the fire.
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds (post-fire and re-recorded deeds); Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum (pre-fire substitute — physical only).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and Civil War draft registrations are at NARA and on Fold3. Illinois state adjutant general records are at the Illinois State Archives.
- **Access:** [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com) (subscription); [NARA](https://www.archives.gov) (free/in-person); Ancestry.com (subscription).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland, Rosehill, Calvary (Catholic), Oak Woods.
- **Online coverage:** [FindAGrave](https://www.findagrave.com) — headstone inscriptions for major Chicago cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemetery offices; not digitized.

### Newspaper records
- **Key resource:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) covers historical Chicago newspapers including the Chicago Tribune, which published extensive coverage of the fire and its aftermath.
- **Research value:** Post-fire newspapers are a prime substitute for missing civil records — published lists of fire victims, relief recipients, and rebuilding property owners can establish residence and family composition during and after the disaster.
- **Physical holdings:** The Newberry Library holds historical Chicago newspaper microfilm.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Chicago received massive waves of Irish, German, Scandinavian, and Eastern European immigrants throughout the 1850s–1890s. Pre-1906 naturalization records could be filed in any court of record; **pre-fire Cook County naturalizations (in the Courthouse) are lost**, but post-fire naturalizations survive at IRAD.
- **Passenger lists:** At NARA and indexed on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch. Primary ports for Midwest-bound immigrants were typically New York, Baltimore, or New Orleans.
- **Access:** Ancestry.com (subscription); FamilySearch (free).

### Tax records
- **Pre-fire status:** Cook County tax rolls were in the Courthouse — **totally destroyed in 1871**.
- **Post-fire records:** Post-1871 tax records may survive at the Cook County Treasurer's office or Illinois State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Federal census schedules and city directories partially replace the destroyed tax records.

### City directories
- **Critical substitute source:** Directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library. They place individuals at a specific address between census years and are the best tool for establishing presence in Chicago in the years the fire erased from civil records. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))*
- **Access:** Newberry Library (most comprehensive); some volumes digitized on Ancestry.com and HathiTrust.

### Fire relief records
- **Post-fire relief:** The Chicago Relief and Aid Society administered relief to fire victims; its records (listing heads of household and family members) may be at the Chicago History Museum.
- **Insurance records:** Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum document pre-fire property ownership — a key substitute source, **physical access only**.

## Records NOT online
- Pre-fire Cook County deeds, probate files, court records, and tax rolls (destroyed 1871; no digital equivalent)
- Chicago Relief and Aid Society fire victim records (Chicago History Museum; not digitized)
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records (Chicago History Museum; not fully digitized)
- Most sexton/burial records for Chicago's major cemeteries
- Archdiocese of Chicago parish registers not included in the FamilySearch church records collection (ID: 1803978)

---

## Known record losses

**The Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871** destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, eliminating:
- All pre-fire deed and land title records
- Pre-fire birth and death registers
- Pre-fire probate records (wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships)
- Pre-fire court records (naturalizations, civil suits, criminal cases)
- Pre-fire tax rolls

**Substitute sources for pre-fire research:**
1. **Federal census 1850, 1860, 1870** (survived; 1870 Chicago is the critical pre-fire snapshot)
2. **FamilySearch Church Records 1833–1925** (collection 1803978, 285K records, indexed + images)
3. **Chicago Title & Trust Company insurance records** → Chicago History Museum (physical)
4. **Burnt Record Act re-recorded deeds (post-1872)** → FamilySearch volume 009982111 (41% indexed); Cook County Recorder (fuller set)
5. **City directories from the 1840s** → Newberry Library
6. **Newspaper archives** (Chicago Tribune and others) → Newspapers.com and Newberry Library

## Research tips

# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (ca. 1855–1900, focus on the Great Fire of 1871)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **County formed:** Cook County, 1831 (place_search dateRange: +1831/)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** No data returned by place_population tool.
- **Economy:** Commerce, meatpacking, grain trade, railroads, manufacturing; Chicago was the primary Midwest rail hub by the 1860s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Heavy waves of Irish, German, Scandinavian, and Eastern European immigrants throughout the 1850s–1890s; ethnic enclaves maintained separate churches and records.
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed ~3.3 square miles, killed ~300 people, left 100,000+ homeless, and wiped out the Cook County Courthouse along with most pre-fire civil records. (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)

## Boundary changes
- Cook County formed 1831; boundaries were stable through the target period.

## ⚠️ Critical context: The Great Fire and record loss

The fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, which housed deeds, birth and death registers, court records (probate, naturalization, civil suits), and tax rolls. The loss is total for most pre-fire county-level civil records. Federal census schedules survived because originals were held in Washington. The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register deeds, creating a partial reconstruction of pre-fire land ownership. Insurance records — especially the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum — became a vital substitute for pre-fire property. City directories from the 1840s onward also survived and are at the Newberry Library.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire; Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)*

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date on FamilySearch:** 1871 — the fire destroyed all earlier county registers. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Illinois Vital Records returned only generic content; a specific statewide registration start date is not confirmed by tool results.
- **What exists on FamilySearch (indexed + images):**
  - Birth Certificates, 1871–1940 — 1,450,000 records (collection ID: 2024189)
  - Death Records, 1871–1947 — 980,000 records (collection ID: 1913456)
  - Marriage Records, 1871–1920 — 620,000 records (collection ID: 1756321)
- **Pre-fire alternative:** Church registers (see below); city directories at the Newberry Library.
- **Where held (originals):** Cook County Clerk's office (vital records from 1871 onward).

### Church records
- **FamilySearch collection:** Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925 — 285,000 records (collection ID: 1803978) — **indexed + images.** This is the primary pre-fire resource, predating the courthouse loss by nearly four decades.
- **Catholic records:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers. Parish registers that survived the fire or were reconstructed by parishes are the best substitute for missing pre-fire civil vital records.
- **Where held (physical):** Archdiocese of Chicago Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives; local parish offices.
- **Language:** Primarily English; some German and Polish registers for immigrant congregations.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Schedules for Cook County/Chicago survive for 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 (1890 was nationally destroyed). **The 1870 Chicago enumeration is the single most important pre-fire source** — it captures the pre-fire population and survived because originals were retained in Washington. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)*
- **Access:** 1850–1880 and 1900 are indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry. 1890 is destroyed nationally.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available 1850–1880; list deaths in the year preceding enumeration. The 1880 mortality schedule may name fire-era victims.

### Probate and court records
- **Pre-fire status:** Probate files, court records, and naturalizations at the Cook County Courthouse were destroyed in 1871. This is a total loss for pre-fire probate.
- **Digitized volumes on FamilySearch (volume_search, totalResults: 2 — complete result set):**
  - imageGroupNumber 009982110 — Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies), 1865–1871, 38 images — **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable → browse-only images**
  - imageGroupNumber 009982111 — Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871–1880, 112 images — **41% name-indexed, not full-text searchable → partially indexed images**
- **Post-fire records:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University holds Cook County records from 1871 onward.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Illinois is a federal (public) land state — rectangular survey system.
- **Pre-fire disaster:** County deed books in the Courthouse were destroyed in 1871. The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required re-registration; Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records serve as substitute evidence for pre-fire ownership. *(Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)*
- **Federal land patents (original grants):** Available at the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) — these were held federally, not in the Courthouse, and survived.
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds (post-fire and re-recorded); Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum (pre-fire substitute).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and Civil War draft registrations at NARA and on Fold3; Illinois state adjutant general records at the Illinois State Archives.
- **Access:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com, subscription); NARA (https://www.archives.gov); Ancestry.com (subscription).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery, Rosehill Cemetery, Calvary Cemetery (Catholic), Oak Woods Cemetery.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) lists headstone inscriptions for major Chicago cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemetery offices; not digitized.

### Newspaper records
- **Key resource:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) covers historical Chicago newspapers including the Chicago Tribune, which published extensive coverage of the fire, its victims, and its aftermath.
- **Research value:** Post-fire newspapers are a prime substitute for missing civil records — published lists of fire victims, relief recipients, and rebuilding property owners can establish residence and family composition.
- **Physical holdings:** Newberry Library holds historical Chicago newspaper microfilm.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Chicago received massive waves of Irish, German, Scandinavian, and Eastern European immigrants throughout the 1850s–1890s. Pre-1906 naturalization records were filed in any court of record; pre-fire Cook County naturalizations are lost, but post-fire naturalizations survive at IRAD.
- **Passenger lists:** At NARA and indexed on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch. Primary ports of entry for Midwest-bound immigrants were typically New York, Baltimore, or New Orleans.
- **Access:** Ancestry.com (subscription); FamilySearch (free).

### Tax records
- **Pre-fire status:** Cook County tax rolls were held in the Courthouse and destroyed in 1871. This is a total loss.
- **Post-fire records:** Post-1871 tax records may survive at the Cook County Treasurer's office or the Illinois State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Federal census schedules and city directories partially replace missing tax records.

### City directories
- **Critical substitute source:** Directories dating from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library. They place individuals at specific addresses between census years and can establish presence before and after the fire. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)*
- **Access:** Newberry Library (Chicago); some digitized on Ancestry.com and HathiTrust.

### Insurance and fire relief records
- **Post-fire relief:** The Chicago Relief and Aid Society administered relief to fire victims; records may list heads of household and family members. Held at the Chicago History Museum.
- **Insurance records:** Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum document pre-fire property ownership and are a key substitute source.

# Locality Guide: French Colonial Louisiana (1699–1769)

## Jurisdictional Context

Louisiana as a **French colony** ran from the founding settlements (~1699) through 1762, when France ceded the territory to Spain by the **Treaty of Fontainebleau**. Spanish governance was not effective until **1769**, so the years 1762–1769 are a transitional gap. If your ancestors lived in Louisiana through the full 1700s, you will cross from French to Spanish colonial record systems — both regimes used the Catholic Church as the primary recorder of vital events, but administrative records shift sharply around 1769.

The colony was **not organized by counties** during this period. Settlement centered on military "posts," plantation districts, and ecclesiastical parishes. There was no civil vital registration. Nearly all genealogically useful records were created by two institutions:
- The **Catholic Church** (baptisms, marriages, burials)
- The **Superior Council / Conseil Supérieur** (the French colonial governing body: land grants, court records, contracts, estate inventories)

---

## Record Types, Repositories & Access

### 1. 🏆 Catholic Parish Registers — PRIMARY SOURCE
**Coverage:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials. The Catholic Church was the **only legally recognized church** in French Louisiana. The *Code Noir* additionally required the baptism of all enslaved persons, making these registers important for African-descended as well as European families.

- **Earliest records:** St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans) has registers beginning **1720**, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)).
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925** (Collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)) — date range 1718–1925, returned by collections_search with ~987,000 records and ~493,000 images. Because collections_search (which surfaces indexed collections) returned this, it is name-searchable on FamilySearch.
- **Physical originals:** St. Louis Cathedral Archives, New Orleans; Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans).
- **Language:** French throughout the colonial period. Records must be read in French — plan accordingly.
- ⚠️ Records from outlying posts (Natchitoches, Mobile district, Illinois Country) may be held at those parishes' own archives or at the Louisiana Historical Center, not exclusively at St. Louis Cathedral.

---

### 2. Superior Council Records (Conseil Supérieur)
**Coverage:** Land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories, civil disputes. This body was the French colonial government's primary administrative and judicial arm.

- **Repository:** **Louisiana Historical Center**, Old U.S. Mint building, 400 Esplanade Ave., New Orleans — holds these records and has partially digitized them.
- **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France — holds administrative correspondence, colonial census rolls, and governor's papers for the colony. Online portal: [anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr). Series **C13A** covers Louisiana.
- **Access:** The ANOM holdings are partially available online; physical access or microfilm for the rest.
- ⚠️ The FamilySearch Wiki notes these records are only *partially* digitized. Assume significant browse-only or physical-only portions remain.

---

### 3. Notarial Records
**Coverage:** Contracts, wills, marriage settlements (*contrats de mariage*), property transactions, emancipations — from the **1730s onward**.

- **Repository:** **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America. Public access is provided on-site.
- Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)), these records document transactions following **French civil law** (not English common law), which is critical for interpreting property and inheritance.
- **Access:** On-site research at the New Orleans Notarial Archives. Some records have been calendared or indexed in published finding aids.
- ⚠️ No FamilySearch online collection for colonial-era notarial records was returned by collections_search — treat as physical/microfilm access only unless otherwise verified.

---

### 4. Land Grants & Concessions
**Coverage:** French-era land concessions (grants of settlement rights from the Crown), documented under French civil law.

- **American State Papers: Public Lands** — documents colonial land grants as they were adjudicated during the early U.S. territorial period. Available via HathiTrust and the Library of Congress.
- **Louisiana State Land Office** — holds surveying and confirmation records for colonial-era grants that were adjudicated after the Louisiana Purchase (1803).
- **ANOM (France)** — original concession records in the colonial administrative correspondence.
- ⚠️ No FamilySearch collection specifically for French colonial land concessions was returned by collections_search.

---

### 5. Colonial Census Rolls
**Coverage:** Periodic censuses of settlers (not regular decennial enumerations). French colonial administrators conducted enumeration rolls of colonists, enslaved persons, and livestock for administrative purposes.

- **Repository:** **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France — per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)).
- **Access:** ANOM online portal; microfilm copies may exist at the Louisiana State Archives or LSU Libraries.
- ⚠️ These are not indexed by FamilySearch. Expect browse-only or physical access.

---

### 6. Probate Records
**Coverage:** Estate inventories, wills, administration records. French legal tradition governed inheritance during the colonial period.

- **FamilySearch collection:** **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984** (Collection [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)) — date range starts **1756**, so covers the final decade of the French colonial period. ~456,000 records and ~228,000 images; returned by collections_search (indexed/name-searchable).
- **Repository for originals:** Louisiana Historical Center; Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge.

---

## FamilySearch Collections Overlapping the French Colonial Period

| Collection | ID | Date Range | Records | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Louisiana, Church Records | [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) | 1718–1925 | ~987,000 | ~493,000 | Indexed + images |
| Louisiana, Probate Records | [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) | 1756–1984 | ~456,000 | ~228,000 | Indexed + images |

> Two other Louisiana collections returned by the search tool — *Parish Marriages, 1837–1957* and *Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964* — do not cover the French colonial period and are post-period context only.

---

## Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Location | Online? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch.org** | Church records (1718+), probate (1756+) | familysearch.org | Yes — indexed |
| **Louisiana Historical Center** | Superior Council records, church record originals, colonial-era documents | Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Partial |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives** | Notarial contracts, wills, marriage settlements (1730s+) | New Orleans, LA | On-site |
| **Louisiana State Archives** | Land, probate, state-era records | Baton Rouge, LA | Partial |
| **LSU Libraries / Hill Memorial Library** | Manuscripts, colonial-era document collections | Baton Rouge, LA | Finding aids online |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)** | Administrative correspondence, census rolls, colonial governance | Aix-en-Provence, France | Partial (anom portal) |
| **Bibliothèque nationale de France (BnF)** | Printed colonial-era sources, maps, some manuscripts | Paris, France / Gallica online | Partial |

---

## Research Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Two colonial regimes overlap the 1700s.** French colonial records run to ~1769; Spanish colonial records begin ~1769. Don't stop at 1762 (the treaty date) — Spanish governance was not effective until 1769, and records in many parishes may not shift until then.
2. **No civil vital registration existed during the French colonial period.** Catholic parish registers are the *only* vital record source. If a baptism, marriage, or burial was not recorded by the Church, it almost certainly was not recorded at all.
3. **Records are in French (and later Spanish).** The colonial church registers and administrative records are in French throughout the target period. Researchers who cannot read 18th-century French script will need a translator.
4. **The Code Noir** required baptism and Catholic marriage of enslaved persons — meaning African and African-descended individuals appear in the same parish registers as free colonists, often with only a given name and the enslaver's surname or first name.
5. **"Parish" means two different things in Louisiana.** In the colonial period, *paroisse* is an ecclesiastical (Catholic) parish. After statehood (1812), Louisiana uses "parish" as its civil county equivalent. The two systems do not perfectly overlap — know which you're searching.
6. **Many records are scattered across two continents.** The primary administrative archive for French colonial Louisiana is in France (ANOM), not in Louisiana. A complete search requires consulting both U.S. and French repositories.
7. **FamilySearch wiki_place_page calls returned only generic content for Louisiana** — the FamilySearch Wiki's locality-specific pages for Louisiana did not load through the tool in this session. Consult [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy) directly for current digitization notes.
8. **FamilySearch volume_search was not run** in this session — additional browse-only digitized volumes beyond the two indexed collections above may exist on FamilySearch and should be checked directly.

---

## Suggested Research Starting Points

1. **Start at FamilySearch** with *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (Collection 1612905) — the broadest digitized, name-indexed source covering the colonial period.
2. **Contact the Louisiana Historical Center** (New Orleans) about Superior Council records for your time window and location.
3. **Search the ANOM online portal** ([anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr)) — Series C13A for Louisiana colonial correspondence and census rolls.
4. **Visit or write to the New Orleans Notarial Archives** for notarial contracts from the 1730s onward.
5. **Check LSU's Louisiana Digital Library** and Hill Memorial Library's manuscript finding aids for transcribed or published colonial-era records.
6. **Published works:** The *Louisiana Colonial Records* volumes (edited by Winston De Ville and others) and the *Sacramental Records of the Roman Catholic Church of the Archdiocese of New Orleans* series are essential secondary finding tools that index many primary sources.

## 🪨 Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Locality Research Guide (c. 1870–1900)

---

### Jurisdictional Overview

Pennsylvania's coal mining region divides into two geographically distinct areas:

- **Anthracite (hard coal) region** — northeastern Pennsylvania, centered on **Schuylkill** (est. 1811), **Luzerne**, **Lackawanna**, **Carbon**, and **Northumberland** counties. According to the Wikipedia article on the [Coal Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region), coal mining expanded dramatically from the 1820s–1870s, drawing large immigrant populations from Ireland, Wales, Germany, and later Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Italy, and Ukraine.
- **Bituminous (soft coal) region** — western Pennsylvania, centered on **Cambria** (est. 1804), **Westmoreland**, **Fayette**, and **Allegheny** counties.

**⚠️ Critical boundary note — Lackawanna County (1878):** Lackawanna County was carved out of Luzerne County in 1878. Any record for the Scranton area *before 1878* — births, deaths, marriages, naturalizations, court filings — was created and is filed under **Luzerne County**. Search Luzerne County records first for that area, then Lackawanna County from 1878 onward. These are one continuous research trail despite the different county names.

---

### Vital Records

The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania vital records and individual county genealogy pages did not return Pennsylvania-specific content in this survey (all resolved to a generic fallback page at `familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records`). **The FamilySearch Wiki does not state a statewide vital registration date in the data retrieved here.** Consult the [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records) wiki page directly for registration start dates. Based on general U.S. practice, Pennsylvania did not have comprehensive *statewide* birth and death registration during the late 1800s, making church records the primary substitute for vital events in this era.

**FamilySearch collections covering marriages (1870–1900):**

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Date Range | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages | [1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) | 1885–1950 | 524,189 | Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages | [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages | [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | Indexed, **no images** |

**Note on death records:** The major FamilySearch death certificate collection ([2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317), 4.2 million records) begins in **1906** — after the target period. For deaths in the late 1800s, church burial registers and mine inspector reports (see below) are the primary substitutes.

---

### Census Records

Federal census enumerations for 1870, 1880, and 1900 cover this region. **The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire** — bridge the gap with the 1880 and 1900 censuses plus local substitutes. Federal census schedules (1870–1900) record occupation as "miner," making them useful for identifying mining families ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)). Mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding each census and can substitute for missing death certificates. The indexed federal census is available at **Ancestry.com** (external link returned in survey).

---

### ⛏️ Occupational & Mining Records (Unique to This Region)

These records are the most distinctive sources for coal mining families and should be searched alongside the standard genealogical record types.

**Pennsylvania State Mine Inspector Reports (1870–):** Published annually from 1870 and held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg). Each report lists fatal mining accidents with the victim's name, age, nationality, and cause of death — making these an irreplaceable substitute for death records for miners killed on the job. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))

**Company employment records** (payrolls, accident reports) survive fragmentarily at the Pennsylvania State Archives and at local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))

**FamilySearch digitized mining volumes** — the volume search matched **23 total digitized volumes** for this region; the first page details 3:

| Volume | imageGroupNumber | Coverage | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County — Mine Worker Employment Cards | 002240015 | Schuylkill, 1870–1900 | 410 | ✅ **95% name-indexed, full-text searchable** |
| Luzerne County — Mine Accident Reports | 002240016 | Luzerne, 1870–1895 | 287 | ⚠️ **Browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) |
| Lackawanna County — Colliery Payroll Ledgers | 002240017 | Lackawanna, 1878–1900 | 199 | ⚠️ **Browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) |

> The Luzerne Mine Accident Reports must be browsed image by image with no name search. The Lackawanna Colliery Payroll Ledgers are the same. **20 additional volumes exist** on subsequent pages and were not detailed in this survey — ask to fetch further pages if needed.

---

### Church Records

Church registers are often the **richest source** for mining families in this era, frequently containing the most detailed family data. The coal region was served by ethnically segregated parishes; identifying your family's likely ethnicity is key to finding the right register:

| Ethnicity | Typical Denomination |
|---|---|
| Irish | Roman Catholic |
| Welsh | Congregational or Baptist |
| German | Lutheran or Roman Catholic |
| Polish / Slovak / Lithuanian | Roman Catholic (ethnic parishes) |
| Ukrainian | Greek Catholic or Orthodox |

Check both local parish archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))

---

### Immigration & Naturalization

Immigration and naturalization records are critical for this population. Many miners arrived through the ports of **Philadelphia** or **New York** and naturalized in county courts near the mines. Before 1906, naturalization petitions could be filed in *any* court of record (not just federal courts). Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) are held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

---

### Union Records

The **United Mine Workers of America (UMWA)**, founded in 1890, maintained membership rolls and grievance files that can document individual miners. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

---

### Probate Records

FamilySearch holds [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) (collection 1999196, 893,214 records, indexed + images). Filed at the county courthouse level.

---

### Military Records

**Fold3** (fold3.com, returned in external link survey) holds military service records and pension files. Given the period, relevant service includes the Civil War (1861–1865) — many mining-age men in the late 1800s were veterans with pension files at the **National Archives** (archives.gov).

---

### Cemetery Records

**Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) was returned as a FamilySearch-curated external resource for this region and period.

---

### Newspapers

**Newspapers.com** was returned as a curated resource. Mining-town papers reported accidents, strikes, union activities, and community news — valuable for names that appear in no other surviving record.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg | Mine Inspector reports from 1870; Schuylkill County naturalizations (1840s–1906); fragmentary company employment records |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County**, Pottsville | Local mining collections and community records |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum**, Scranton | Mining community records for the northeastern anthracite region |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Digitized marriages, probate, and mining-specific volumes (23+ volumes identified) |
| **Ancestry.com** | Indexed federal census collections |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Passenger lists; military service and pension records |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Military records |
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers from mining communities |

---

### ⚠️ Research Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Lackawanna County records before 1878 are under Luzerne County.** Search Luzerne first for any event in the Scranton area before 1878; switch to Lackawanna from 1878 onward.
2. **No statewide vital registration in the late 1800s.** Church records and mine inspector reports are the primary substitutes for birth and death certificates in this period.
3. **The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed.** Bridge the 20-year gap between 1880 and 1900 with church records, state/local tax lists, city directories, and mining company records.
4. **Identify the ethnic parish before searching church records.** Different nationalities worshipped at separate congregations; records are not consolidated by geography but by denomination and ethnicity.
5. **Mine Inspector reports are a unique death-record substitute.** For any miner who died on the job from 1870 forward, check the annual Pennsylvania Mine Inspector reports before concluding no death record exists.
6. **Browse-only volumes require image-by-image searching.** The Luzerne Mine Accident Reports and Lackawanna Colliery Payroll Ledgers at FamilySearch are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — you must page through them manually.
7. **23 digitized volumes exist; only 3 detailed here.** Additional FamilySearch mining-region volumes are on subsequent pages and were not retrieved in this survey — ask if you need the full list.
8. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered.** Before September 1906, any court could naturalize — check county court records in whichever county the miner lived, not just federal courts.
