## 📍 Locality Research Guide: Massachusetts, United States | c. 1620–1700

### Jurisdictional Overview

The early 1600s in Massachusetts spans **two separate colonial jurisdictions**, which is the single most important research fact for this period:

| Colony | Active | Counties |
|---|---|---|
| **Plymouth Colony** | 1620–1691 | Plymouth, Bristol, Barnstable (formed 1685) |
| **Massachusetts Bay Colony** | 1628/1630–1691 | Suffolk, Middlesex, Essex, Norfolk (formed 1643) |

Both colonies merged in 1691 to form the **Province of Massachusetts Bay**. Records, court systems, and land administration were completely separate until that date. A family near Plymouth required different record sets than one near Boston.

⚠️ **Critical quirk:** County formation in 1643 (Suffolk, Middlesex, Essex, Norfolk) means pre-1643 deed and probate records are held at the colony level in the Massachusetts Archives — not at a county courthouse.

---

### Record Types, Availability & Access

#### 1. 🗂️ Town Vital Records — **Indexed + Images on FamilySearch**

- **What they contain:** Births, marriages, deaths recorded by town clerks
- **Start date:** Town-level recording mandated by the colony in **1639** — one of the earliest civil registration requirements in North America. This is a **town-level** mandate only; statewide registration did not begin until the 19th century.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — name-indexed, ~3.46 million records
- **Published finding tool:** The multi-volume *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* (Tanner–Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns — search this series **before** going to originals
- **Originals held at:** Town clerk offices and Massachusetts Archives, Boston
- **Gap:** Events before 1639 have no civil registration; use church records as primary substitute

#### 2. ⛪ Church (Congregational) Records — **Indexed + Images on FamilySearch**

- **What they contain:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership lists, disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments)
- **Why essential:** The Congregational church was the established church of both colonies. Church records are often the **only** source for events before 1639 and remain the best corroborating source throughout the period
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — name-indexed, ~988,000 records
- **Published sources:** Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications have transcribed many early registers
- **Unpublished manuscripts:** New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston — largest genealogical research library in New England; holds extensive manuscript church record collections
- **Originals held at:** Individual congregational church archives and NEHGS

#### 3. 📜 Probate Records — **Indexed + Images on FamilySearch**

- **What they contain:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships
- **Start date:** County probate courts operating from **1635**
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — name-indexed, ~568,000 records
- **Held at:** County probate courts and Massachusetts Archives
- **Note:** Pre-1643 probate records (before county formation) are at the Massachusetts Archives under colony-level administration — not at county courthouses

#### 4. 🏠 Land & Deed Records — **Physical/County + Massachusetts Archives**

- **What they contain:** Deeds, land grants, patent records documenting land ownership and transfers
- **Start date:** County deed recording from **1630s**; colony-level land grants from 1620s
- **Coverage:** Deed books survive in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds from 1643 onward
- **Held at:** County Registries of Deeds (county-level from 1643); Massachusetts Archives holds colony-era grants (pre-1643)
- **FamilySearch digitization:** No specific land/deed collection returned for this period — consult the Massachusetts Archives directly; some county deed books may be on microfilm at FamilySearch

#### 5. ⚖️ Colonial Court Records — **Massachusetts Archives (physical)**

- **What they contain:** Court of Assistants, County Courts, General Court proceedings — include family relationships, guardianships, property disputes, criminal cases
- **Why useful:** Court records frequently name family members and establish relationships not found in vital records
- **Held at:** Massachusetts Archives, Boston — holds colonial court records from the 1620s onward
- **FamilySearch digitization:** Not returned as a FamilySearch collection for this period

#### 6. 🛳️ Great Migration / Immigration Records — **NEHGS + Published Series**

- **What they contain:** Documentation of every known settler arriving in New England 1620–1643
- **Key resource:** *The Great Migration Study Series* (NEHGS) — the premier secondary source for identifying and verifying immigrant ancestors; covers ~20,000 settlers in the 1630–1640 Great Migration
- **Available at:** AmericanAncestors.org (NEHGS subscription) and major research libraries
- **FamilySearch gap:** FamilySearch Passenger Lists begin **1820** — no digitized passenger lists cover the colonial arrival period on FamilySearch

#### 7. 📊 Census Substitutes (No Federal Census Until 1790)

- **What to use instead:** Tax lists, militia lists, freeman rolls, and town inhabitant lists
- **Held at:** Massachusetts Archives, Boston; some published in historical society volumes
- **Note:** The first federal census is 1790 — nothing on FamilySearch substitutes for colonial census records for this period

#### 8. 🪦 Cemetery Records

- **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com): Covers some colonial-era burial grounds; many early Puritan gravestones are documented
- **Physical:** Colonial-era burying grounds (17th century) are found in most original Massachusetts towns; many stones survive

---

### Plymouth Colony — Search Separately

Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) had a completely independent record system from Massachusetts Bay Colony. Its records have been published and indexed separately in multi-volume sets. **If your ancestor lived in Plymouth, Bristol, or Barnstable county towns, you must search the Plymouth Colony record series independently — do not rely solely on Massachusetts Bay Colony searches.**

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What's Held | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives**, Boston | Colony records, court records, tax lists, militia lists, colonial grants | [sec.state.ma.us](https://www.sec.state.ma.us/arc/) — in person and online finding aids |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)**, Boston | Great Migration series, manuscript church records, published genealogies | [americanancestors.org](https://www.americanancestors.org) — subscription + in-person |
| **FamilySearch.org** | 3 indexed collections (town vitals, church records, probate); free | [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |
| **County Registries of Deeds** | Deed books from 1643 onward | County courthouse; some on microfilm at FamilySearch |
| **County Probate Courts** | Probate records from 1635 | County courthouse; FamilySearch collection covers many |
| **Ancestry.com** | Massachusetts vital records; some indexed colonial records | Subscription |
| **NARA** (National Archives) | Federal records — primarily post-1776 for this locality | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) |

---

### Research Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Two separate colonies.** Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691) were entirely separate jurisdictions with separate courts, land systems, and record sets. Always determine which colony your ancestor lived in before searching.
2. **Pre-county records at the colony level.** Suffolk, Middlesex, Essex, and Norfolk counties formed in 1643. Pre-1643 deed and probate records are held at the colony level in the Massachusetts Archives, not at any county courthouse.
3. **Town-level vital registration from 1639 only.** The 1639 mandate is a town-level requirement; statewide registration did not begin until the 1840s. For events before 1639, church records are the primary substitute.
4. **Start with the Tanner-Corbin series.** The *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* published series covers 200+ towns and is the standard finding tool — search it before the original town clerk records.

# 🗺️ Oklahoma Locality Guide — Land Run of 1889 & Oklahoma Territory (c. 1885–1910)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Understanding Oklahoma's three-tier jurisdictional history is the single most important thing you can do before searching — it controls which records exist and where they are held.

| Period | Jurisdiction | Civil Infrastructure |
|---|---|---|
| Before April 22, 1889 | Unassigned Lands / Indian Territory | None for settlers; tribal nations only |
| Apr 22, 1889 – May 1, 1890 | Unassigned Lands (no organized territory) | **Federal land offices only** (Guthrie & Kingfisher) — no county courts, no civil vital registration |
| May 2, 1890 – Nov 15, 1907 | Oklahoma Territory (western) + Indian Territory (eastern, separate) | Territorial courts, county records begin; Indian Territory kept entirely separate records |
| Nov 16, 1907 onward | State of Oklahoma | County and state records; statewide vital registration (Oct 1908) |

> ⚠️ **Critical temporal split:** For the first year after the Land Run (April 1889 – May 1890), **no county governments, county courts, or civil vital records existed.** The only documentary trace of a Land Run family in that window is a federal homestead or town-lot filing.

---

## 1. Land & Homestead Records ⭐ START HERE

**The single richest record class for Land Run families.** Every settler who filed a homestead claim created a federal file that can run 10–30 pages.

**What each file contains:**
- Original homestead application (name, age, nativity, prior residence)
- Proof of settlement — a sworn statement with **two witnesses** (often neighbors, themselves searchable)
- Final certificate / land patent
- Rejected or contested applications also survive and contain the same family detail

**Repositories:**
- **National Archives, Washington D.C.** — Record Group 49 (General Land Office). The original homestead case files.
- **BLM General Land Office Records** — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — free, searchable database of Oklahoma land patents. Search by name to confirm the claim, then order the full case file from NARA.
- **FamilySearch** — *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* (Collection [1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)) — 234,567 indexed records with 117,283 images. **Digitized and name-indexed.**
- **Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS), Oklahoma City** — holds land run claim files, town lot records, and supplementary territorial land records.

**Source:** [FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Land Records, Land Run section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)

---

## 2. Vital Records — Major Gap; Use Substitutes

Oklahoma **statewide civil vital registration did not begin until October 1908**, and compliance remained poor through the 1930s. There are **no civil birth, marriage, or death records** for the Land Run period or the territorial era (1889–1907).

| Record Type | Earliest Availability | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| Birth certificates | Oct 1908 (statewide, poor compliance pre-1930) | Oklahoma State Archives |
| Death certificates | Oct 1908 | Oklahoma State Archives |
| County marriages | May 2, 1890 (counties established) | County courthouses; FamilySearch collection [2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789) |

**FamilySearch — Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995** (Collection [2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789)): 456,789 records / 913,578 persons — **digitized and name-indexed.** Marriage is often the first county-level document a Land Run family generated.

**Source:** [FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Vital Records, Registration History](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records#Registration_History)

**Vital-record substitutes for 1889–1908:**
- Church registers (see §5 below)
- Census records (see §3 below)
- Cemetery records — [FindAGrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)
- Newspaper birth/marriage/death notices — [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com); territorial newspapers began in Guthrie and other towns almost immediately after April 1889

---

## 3. Census Records

| Census | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1880 federal census | Departure states (Kansas, Texas, Missouri, etc.) | Search here to find the family *before* the Land Run |
| **1890 Oklahoma Territory special census** | Oklahoma Territory only | **One of the only surviving 1890 census records in the nation** — nearly all 1890 federal schedules were destroyed. Held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society**. |
| 1900 federal census | Oklahoma Territory + Indian Territory (enumerated separately) | Available at NARA and FamilySearch |
| 1907 Dawes/Statehood census | Indian Territory tribal citizens | Tied to Dawes rolls (see §6) |
| 1910 federal census | State of Oklahoma (first post-statehood census) | Available at NARA and FamilySearch |

> The 1890 OT special census is a rare gift — most families who ran in 1889 appear in it. Prioritize it.

---

## 4. Territorial & County Court Records (1890–1907)

Oklahoma Territory's territorial district courts handled civil cases, criminal cases, probate, and **naturalizations** (pre-1906 naturalizations could occur in any court of record).

**Repositories:**
- **National Archives at Fort Worth, TX** — primary repository for Oklahoma and Indian Territory federal district court records, 1890–1907. [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)
- **Oklahoma State Archives, Oklahoma City** — additional territorial court records
- **County courthouses** — probate, deed books, and local court records from May 1890 onward

**Source:** [FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Territorial Records, Courts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

---

## 5. Church Records

Denominations established congregations in new Oklahoma Territory towns almost immediately after April 1889 — Baptist, Methodist, and Catholic congregations are documented from the first months. Church registers substitute for absent civil vital records.

**FamilySearch** — *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* (Collection [1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)): 123,456 records / 61,728 images — **digitized and name-indexed.**

**Denominational archives:**
- **Oklahoma Conference of the United Methodist Church Archives** — Methodist congregation records
- **Diocese of Oklahoma City** — Catholic parish registers
- Local Baptist association archives

---

## 6. Indian Territory & Tribal Records

Oklahoma Territory (western, organized) and Indian Territory (eastern, Five Civilized Tribes) had **entirely separate record systems** until statehood in 1907. If your ancestor lived in or near eastern Oklahoma, these records are essential — even for non-tribal settlers who interacted with tribal courts and land systems.

**FamilySearch** — *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* (Collection [1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)): 567,890 records / 283,945 images — **digitized and name-indexed.**

**Dawes Commission Rolls (1898–1914):** documented citizenship in the Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, and Seminole nations. Essential for tribal families; also relevant to non-citizens who appeared in related records. Held at NARA and indexed on FamilySearch.

**Missionary church records** for the Five Civilized Tribes predate territorial settlement and are among the earliest records in the region.

---

## 7. Military Records

Many Land Run participants were Civil War veterans. **Pension files** are among the most genealogically rich federal records — they often name spouses, children, birth places, and dates.

- **National Archives, Washington D.C.** — service records, pension files, bounty land warrants
- **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) — digitized military records, searchable by subscription
- **Oklahoma Adjutant General records** (Spanish-American War, WWI era) — Oklahoma State Archives

---

## 8. Newspapers

Oklahoma Territory had a thriving newspaper press almost from Day 1. The *Oklahoma State Capital* (Guthrie) began publication in 1889. Territorial papers carried land run notices, homestead contest announcements, social columns, and vital notices.

- **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)) — subscription; broad historical Oklahoma holdings
- **Oklahoma Historical Society newspaper collection** — check their digital holdings

---

## 9. Departure-State Research — Essential Step

The FamilySearch Wiki notes that **many Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and Arkansas.** Because no civil records exist for 1889–1890 Oklahoma Territory, you will often need to reconstruct a family's origins entirely from departure-state records before finding them on the claim.

**Strategy:**
1. Find the family in the 1890 OT special census or 1900 federal census — note stated birthplace and age
2. Work backward in the **1880 federal census** for Kansas, Texas, Missouri, or wherever the birthplace and age point
3. Trace county records in those states to establish parentage, siblings, and prior land ownership

---

## Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** (Oklahoma City) | 1890 OT special census, land run claim files, town lot records, early county records, territorial newspapers | In-person & some digital via OHS website |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** (Oklahoma City) | Birth/death records from Oct 1908+, state records, territorial records | In-person; partial online |
| **National Archives, Washington D.C.** | RG 49 — General Land Office homestead case files | In-person; order microfilm; some digitized on FamilySearch |
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** | Oklahoma/Indian Territory federal court records, 1890–1907 | In-person; partial microfilm |
| **BLM GLO Records** | Land patent database | Free — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) |
| **FamilySearch** | Collections 1541872, 1987432, 2134789, 1654321 | Free — familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census collections | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military records | Subscription |

---

## Key Quirks to Know

1. **No civil records before May 2, 1890.** For the first year after the Land Run, the homestead file is the only paper trail. County records, county courts, and county marriages all start May 2, 1890.
2. **The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census survived** — a rare exception to the nationwide destruction of 1890 schedules. It is at the Oklahoma Historical Society and is a crucial early enumeration.
3. **Oklahoma vital registration didn't begin until October 1908**, with poor compliance until the 1930s. Church registers, census records, and newspapers are the primary substitutes for 1889–1908 vital events.
4. **Oklahoma Territory (west) and Indian Territory (east) had entirely separate record systems** until statehood November 16, 1907. Establish which territory your ancestor lived in before searching — the collections don't overlap.
5. **Homestead case files at NARA (RG 49) are the richest source** for Land Run families — each file includes the application, settlement proof with neighbor-witnesses, and the final patent, all containing biographical detail.
6. **Rejected and contested homestead claims also survive** and can contain even more detail (affidavits, testimony, character witnesses).
7. **Trace the family in departure states first** (Kansas, Texas, Missouri, Arkansas) using the 1880 federal census before searching Oklahoma records — it will anchor the search to a specific family unit.
8. **BLM GLO Records** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) is a free name-indexed starting point to confirm a patent, then order the full case file from NARA.

---

**Suggested search order for a Land Run family:**
1. BLM GLO Records → confirm the land patent claim
2. FamilySearch collection 1541872 → early land records (indexed)
3. OHS 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census
4. 1900 federal census (FamilySearch / Ancestry)
5. FamilySearch collection 2134789 → county marriages from 1890
6. National Archives at Fort Worth → territorial court records
7. Church records (collection 1654321 + denominational archives)
8. Departure-state 1880 census and county records to establish origins

# Locality Research Guide: Alabama Region, c. 1780–1819 (Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdictional Context

The territory that became Alabama passed through **four sovereign authorities** before statehood, each leaving a distinct documentary trail:

| Period | Sovereign / Jurisdiction | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | **French Louisiana** (Mobile Bay area) | Fort Louis de la Mobile founded 1702 |
| 1763–1780 | **British West Florida** | Mobile ceded to Britain after Seven Years' War |
| 1780–1813 | **Spanish West Florida** (Mobile District) | Spain seized Mobile 1780; U.S. took Mobile 1813 |
| 1798–1817 | **Mississippi Territory** | Present-day Alabama was the eastern half |
| 1817–1819 | **Alabama Territory** | Separated from Mississippi Territory |
| 1819– | **State of Alabama** | Admitted December 14, 1819 |

**Critical research consequence:** Records created before 1817 are filed under the **Mississippi Territory**, not Alabama. Most FamilySearch indexes and finding aids will not surface them under an Alabama search — you must search the Mississippi Territory and Mississippi state collections simultaneously.

The **interior** of present-day Alabama was largely Creek and Cherokee territory until after the Creek War of 1813–1814. American settler records for the interior are sparse before 1814; most pre-1814 American records concentrate around the **Tombigbee River settlements** (Washington and Baldwin Counties, est. 1800) and the **Tennessee Valley** (Madison County, est. 1809). The Mobile Bay area has the deepest continuous documentary record, going back to French colonial settlement.

---

## Record Types Available for This Period

### 1. Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**There was no civil vital registration in this period.** No territorial or state-mandated recording of births or deaths existed. The FamilySearch wiki pages for Alabama Vital Records, Alabama Genealogy, Alabama Church Records, Alabama Census, and Alabama Probate Records all returned only generic fallback content when fetched by URL — no Alabama-specific registration dates or details could be retrieved from those pages. For vital events c. 1800, you must use substitutes:

- **Church registers** (see below) are the primary vital substitute
- **Tax lists** can document a person's presence year to year as a proxy for survival
- **Territorial census substitutes** record heads of household

**Marriage records** begin with county formation. FamilySearch holds the indexed collection **"Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950"** (Collection [1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408)), which includes 612,345 records with 306,172 associated images. This collection starts in **1809**, when the first Alabama counties were organized — no indexed Alabama county marriages predate county formation.

> 🔍 **Access level:** Indexed + images (searchable by name)

---

### 2. Territorial Census Substitutes

The wiki_search confirmed that **Mississippi Territory census enumerations** were conducted in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810**, enumerating settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy, Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))

FamilySearch holds two relevant indexed collections:

- **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** (Collection [2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756)): 287,634 records, **no images**. The earliest entries (1810) are the Mississippi Territory federal census schedules for the Alabama portion.
- **"Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890"** (Collection [1927171](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171)): 198,340 records, **no images**. Covers the territorial-era enumeration years 1792–1819 and would include pre-statehood Alabama settlers filed under the Mississippi Territory.

> 🔍 **Access level (both):** Name-indexed only — no images attached. Physical originals or transcriptions required for full record detail.

The **federal census of 1810** is the first to enumerate present-day Alabama as part of the Mississippi Territory. The 1800 federal census did not cover this area in a surviving schedule. The 1820 federal census is the first under Alabama statehood.

---

### 3. Land Records

Alabama is a **federal land state**: the U.S. government surveyed and distributed land through the General Land Office (GLO). This makes federal land patents the foundation of pre-county land documentation.

**Key resource:** The **Bureau of Land Management (BLM) General Land Office Records** website ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) holds digitized federal land patents for Alabama, including early grants from the territorial period. These are name-searchable and free.

FamilySearch holds **"Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907"** (Collection [1919694](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694)): 312,450 records with 156,225 images. This collection begins in **1798** (the year the Mississippi Territory was established) and covers the entire territorial period for what is now Alabama. Because the collection is indexed under Mississippi state scope, pre-statehood Alabama land records are mixed within it — search this collection alongside any Alabama-specific search.

> 🔍 **Access level:** Indexed + images

**Colonial land grants (Mobile area):**
- **Spanish land grants** (1780–1813) for the Mobile District are held at the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville, Spain, with copies at the **Library of Congress**. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **French colonial land records** are at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer** in Aix-en-Provence, France, with microfilm copies at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**.

These colonial grants are **not digitized or indexed on FamilySearch** — physical or microfilm access is required.

**Tax lists** from the territorial period (land tax, poll tax) survive for some counties at ADAH and serve as both land and census substitutes. The wiki_search confirmed these are among the territorial records at ADAH, though FamilySearch does not show a dedicated indexed collection for them in this window.

---

### 4. Probate Records

FamilySearch holds **"Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985"** (Collection [1537764](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764)): 438,210 records with 219,105 images. This begins in **1809** with the first Alabama county courts. Wills, estate inventories, and guardianship files from this collection's earliest years overlap with the final decade of the territorial period.

> 🔍 **Access level:** Indexed + images

No separate probate collection for the Mississippi Territory period (pre-1809 Alabama counties) was returned by the tools. Territorial-era probate matters would have been handled at the territorial district court level; records from Washington County (est. 1800) and Baldwin County (est. 1809) are the earliest available.

---

### 5. Church Records

Church registers are the **single most important vital substitute** for this period and predate all civil registration by decades.

- **Catholic registers** for the Mobile area (the oldest continuous settlement) begin in the French period and continue through Spanish and American administration. FamilySearch holds **"Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950"** (Collection [1986396](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396)): 156,789 records with 78,394 images.
- **"Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950"** (Collection [2034891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891)): 87,654 records with 43,827 images. Territorial-era Alabama church entries may appear in this Mississippi collection.

> 🔍 **Access level (both):** Indexed + images

**French and Spanish Catholic registers** for Mobile (pre-1813) exist at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer** and **Archivo General de Indias** respectively, with microfilm at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**. These are **not in FamilySearch's digitized or indexed holdings** — physical or microfilm access required.

Protestant congregations (Methodist, Baptist) began organizing in the Tombigbee settlements c. 1808–1815. Their earliest registers, where they survive, are held by local churches, denominational archives, or ADAH.

---

### 6. Court Records

Territorial court records (district courts established under the Mississippi Territory) include litigation, guardian bonds, naturalization petitions, and miscellaneous civil matters. The wiki_search identified these among territorial records at **ADAH**. FamilySearch holds **"Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920"** (Collection [1855293](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293)): 245,670 records with 122,835 images, beginning 1799 — this Mississippi-scope collection may contain territorial-era records from the Alabama district courts.

> 🔍 **Access level:** Indexed + images (Mississippi scope — pre-statehood Alabama records filed here)

---

### 7. Military Records

This period encompasses several military events generating surviving documentation:

- **Creek War, 1813–1814**: Service records and pension files at **NARA** (Record Group 94). [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) holds digitized Creek War records.
- **War of 1812**: Territorial militia service records at NARA. Many Alabama Territory settlers served.
- **Spanish colonial militia records** (Mobile, 1780–1813): At the **Archivo General de Indias**, with some copies at the **Library of Congress** and **Mobile Municipal Archives**.

NARA is the primary repository for federal military records of this era. Fold3 was returned as a curated external link for this place/period.

---

### 8. Colonial Records (Mobile Area, Pre-1813)

This is a **specialist research area** requiring work in European archives:

- **French period (1702–1763):** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives
- **British period (1763–1780):** Colonial Office records at The National Archives (Kew, UK); some in Library of Congress
- **Spanish period (1780–1813):** Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress

These colonial records include census returns, church registers, land grants, and administrative correspondence. None appeared in FamilySearch's digitized or indexed holdings via the tools used here.

---

## Digitized Browse-Only Volumes

**The volume_search tool returned zero results** for both "Alabama, United States" and "Mississippi Territory, United States" for the years 1780–1820. FamilySearch's Records Management Service does not currently show digitized image-only (browse-only) volumes filed under either place designation for this window.

This is a **real gap**, not a blanket absence of digitization: the indexed collections above do include images (county marriages, probate, church records, land records) but those were created from 1803 or 1809 onward. Pre-county territorial materials — tax lists, militia rolls, territorial court minutebooks, the 1801/1805/1808 census enumerations — do not appear in FamilySearch's digitized holdings based on these results.

**What to browse instead:**
- **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** digital collections at [archives.alabama.gov](https://archives.alabama.gov) hold a range of territorial-era volumes online, including territorial legislative records and early court minutes.
- **BLM GLO website** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) has browsable and searchable Alabama federal land patents from the territorial period.
- The **Library of Congress** ([loc.gov](https://loc.gov)) holds microfilmed Spanish colonial records with some digitization.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Alabama ADAH, Montgomery** | Territorial censuses (1801–1810), tax lists, militia rolls, territorial court records, county records |
| **NARA (Washington, D.C. / Atlanta)** | Federal land patents, military service/pension records, 1810 federal census |
| **BLM General Land Office** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) | Federal land patents, Alabama territorial entries |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | Microfilm of French and Spanish colonial records |
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville** | Spanish colonial records (census, church, land grants) |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence** | French colonial records |
| **FamilySearch** ([familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org)) | County marriages (from 1809), probate (from 1809), church records (from 1803), land records (from 1798, Mississippi scope) |
| **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) | Creek War, War of 1812, military pension records |

---

## Research Quirks — Things You Must Know

1. **Pre-1817 Alabama records are filed under Mississippi Territory.** When searching FamilySearch or any other repository, you must search under Mississippi (not Alabama) for records created before Alabama Territory was organized in 1817. The collections_search for Mississippi Territory resolved to Mississippi state scope, meaning pre-statehood Alabama entries are intermingled with Mississippi state records.

2. **No Alabama counties existed until 1800 (Washington) and 1809 (Madison).** Most FamilySearch Alabama county collections begin in 1809 or later. For research in the Tombigbee settlements, Washington County (est. 1800) is the earliest Alabama-side jurisdiction.

3. **The interior was Native American territory until 1814.** The Creek War of 1813–1814 opened the interior for American settlement. American genealogical records for interior Alabama are essentially nonexistent before 1814. If your ancestor was in "Alabama" around 1800, they were almost certainly in the Mobile/Tombigbee corridor or the extreme north (Tennessee Valley).

4. **Mobile area records require European archive access.** French and Spanish Catholic registers and land records for Mobile are in archives in Aix-en-Provence and Seville, not on FamilySearch. Microfilm copies exist at the Mobile Municipal Archives.

5. **The 4 wiki_place_page sections and 6 wiki_read fetches for Alabama-specific pages all returned generic fallback content** — the FamilySearch Wiki's Alabama-specific pages (Alabama_Vital_Records, Alabama_Genealogy, Alabama_Land_and_Property, etc.) did not resolve through the tool. Consult those pages directly at familysearch.org/wiki for additional detail not captured here.

6. **Tax lists are a critical census substitute.** For years between territorial enumerations, county tax lists (beginning with each county's formation) are the best year-by-year proof of a person's presence and approximate wealth/landholding.

7. **Federal land state — no county deed books for the first grant.** In Alabama, the original transfer from the U.S. government to the first private owner is documented in the federal patent (at BLM GLO), not in county deed books. County deed books only record subsequent transfers.

8. **Statewide vital registration came much later.** The FamilySearch wiki pages for Alabama Vital Records did not return Alabama-specific content through the tool. Do not assume any statewide birth or death registration for this period — there was none.

---

## Summary: What's Searchable Online vs. What Requires a Trip

| Record Type | Period | Online & Indexed | Browse-Only Digitized | Physical/Microfilm Only |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Federal land patents | 1798–1819 | ✅ BLM GLO | — | — |
| County marriages | 1809–1819 | ✅ FamilySearch | — | — |
| Probate records | 1809–1819 | ✅ FamilySearch | — | — |
| Church records | 1803–1819 | ✅ FamilySearch | — | — |
| Territorial land records | 1798–1819 | ✅ FamilySearch (MS scope) | — | — |
| MS Territory court records | 1799–1819 | ✅ FamilySearch (MS scope) | — | — |
| Territorial census substitutes | 1801–1810 | ✅ Index only, no images | — | ADAH (originals) |
| Spanish colonial records | 1780–1813 | — | — | ✅ Seville / LOC / Mobile |
| French colonial records | 1702–1763 | — | — | ✅ Aix-en-Provence / Mobile |
| Tax lists / militia rolls | 1800–1819 | — | — | ✅ ADAH |
| Browse-only FS image volumes | 1780–1820 | — | **0 found** | — |

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860s–1890s)
### Counties: Schuylkill · Luzerne · Lackawanna · Carbon · Northumberland · Columbia

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Schuylkill County formed** | 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties |
| **County seat (Schuylkill)** | Pottsville |
| **Population — Schuylkill County** | 89,510 (1860) → 116,428 (1870) → 129,974 (1880) → 172,927 (1900) |
| **Economy** | Anthracite ("hard coal") mining dominated all six counties; world's primary anthracite source in this period |
| **Ethnic composition** | Large Irish Catholic immigrant community; Welsh and English miners; German settlers; Eastern European immigrants arriving after ~1880 |
| **Religious denominations** | Roman Catholic (most Irish immigrants); Welsh Congregational and Calvinist Methodist; Episcopal; Lutheran; Reformed; Methodist Episcopal; Presbyterian |
| **Key events** | Molly Maguires trials 1875–1877 (Schuylkill County); Long Strike of 1875; Diocese of Scranton formed 1868; Lackawanna County carved from Luzerne County |

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Schuylkill County:** Formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; boundaries stable through the target period. [FamilySearch place_search_all]
- **Lackawanna County:** Carved from Luzerne County. **Critical:** Any event in the Scranton/Lackawanna area *before Lackawanna County's formation* must be sought under **Luzerne County** records. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for both Luzerne and Lackawanna counties returned generic content in this session — consult those pages directly on familysearch.org to confirm the exact formation date.
- **Columbia County:** Not listed among the five core anthracite counties (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, Carbon) in the FamilySearch Wiki *Pennsylvania Coal Region Records* page. Confirm whether your ancestor's community falls within the anthracite field proper before applying coal-region strategies.

---

## ⛏ Specialized Coal-Region Indexes

> **Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)**

### Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898
- Names approximately **41,000 colliery workers** across the lower anthracite field.
- Drawn from company payroll books that survived a **1903 records consolidation** — most payroll books were destroyed in that consolidation; this index is the surviving fraction.
- Each entry includes: **occupation** (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), **wage rate**, and **parish of origin** where stated.
- **This is the most direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners** whose names were indexed inconsistently in census records. Search it before the census for anyone in the Lackawanna/Luzerne field.

### Pennsylvania Triennial Tax Assessments (from 1853)
- Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents on a **triennial (every three years)** cycle from 1853.
- Ledgers list: householder name, real estate value, **occupation**, and **nativity** (place of birth — valuable for confirming Irish origin).
- Fills intercensal gaps; partially compensates for the destruction of the 1890 federal census.

### Catholic Parish Survival
- Many Catholic parishes in the coal region were established 1840–1870 for Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities.
- **Diocese of Scranton** (established 1868): holds baptismal registers for coal-region Catholic parishes **post-1868**.
- **Diocese of Harrisburg**: holds registers for coal-region Catholic parishes **pre-1868**.
- **Key quirk:** Searching only the Diocese of Scranton misses all pre-1868 Catholic events in the Lackawanna/Luzerne field.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Registration dates:** Pennsylvania statewide civil registration dates were not confirmed by the tools in this session (the Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page returned generic content). Consult [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records) directly.
- **Death Records on FamilySearch:** Pennsylvania Death Records 1852–1968 — **674 images, 0% indexed, browse-only** (image group 008120442, PA-state level).
- **Marriage Records on FamilySearch:** Schuylkill County Marriage Records 1870–1910 — **94 images, 0% indexed, browse-only** (image group 007936753).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers (Diocese of Harrisburg pre-1868, Diocese of Scranton post-1868); county orphans' court records; newspaper notices.

### Church Records
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic (primary for Irish immigrants); Welsh Congregational and Calvinist Methodist; Episcopal; Lutheran; Reformed; Presbyterian.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:**
  - Catholic (pre-1868): Diocese of Harrisburg Archives, Harrisburg PA
  - Catholic (post-1868): Diocese of Scranton Archives, Scranton PA
  - FamilySearch: Schuylkill County Church Records 1842–1895 — **187 images, 0% indexed, browse-only**, languages **English and German** (image group 007936751)
  - FamilySearch collections: "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708–1985) — **labeled "synthetic test fixture" in its title; verify actual contents before relying on it**
- **Language note:** German-language records appear in the Schuylkill County church volume alongside English ones — German immigrant congregations coexisted with Irish Catholic and Welsh Protestant communities.

### Census Records
- **Federal census:** Available for all six counties — 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 (1890 largely destroyed; see Record Losses).
- **Mortality schedules:** 1860, 1870, 1880 — record deaths in the prior 12 months; valuable for death data before civil registration.
- **Union veterans schedule:** 1880 included a special Union veterans and widows schedule.
- **Pennsylvania state census:** No state census series for this period returned by FamilySearch tools.
- **Access:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 censuses indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and Court Records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions (Orphans' Court); naturalizations, civil and criminal matters (Court of Common Pleas / Quarter Sessions).
- **FamilySearch — Schuylkill County:** Probate Records 1851–1930 — **412 images, 0% indexed, browse-only** (image group 007936749).
- **FamilySearch — PA state:** Probate Records 1683–1994 — **1,180 images, 0% indexed, browse-only** (image group 008120441); also collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994, 2.3M images, **no person index, browse-only**).
- **Naturalization Records (critical for Irish immigrants):**
  - Schuylkill County: 1849–1915, **298 images, 0% indexed, browse-only** (image group 007936750)
  - PA state level: 1790–1915, **351 images, 15% indexed** (image group 008120443)
  - Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — check county Courts of Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, and federal district courts.

### Land Records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state; metes-and-bounds descriptions.
- **FamilySearch:** Schuylkill County Deed Records 1815–1900 — **543 images, 22% indexed** (image group 007936752) — the most name-searchable FamilySearch land record for this region.
- **Where held:** Recorder of Deeds at each county courthouse.
- **Note:** Pennsylvania Land and Property wiki page returned generic content; consult [Pennsylvania Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property) directly.

### Military Records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); many Irish coal miners served in Pennsylvania volunteer infantry regiments.
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files (NARA RG 94/15); Civil War draft registrations 1863 (NARA); PA adjutant general records at Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Access:** Indexed on Fold3 and Ancestry; some on FamilySearch. Grand Army of the Republic (GAR) post records at PA State Archives and county historical societies.

### Cemetery Records
- **Types:** Denominational (Catholic, Protestant) and company-managed burial grounds present in each coal town.
- **Online:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves cover many coal-region cemeteries; coverage incomplete for rural mining patches and company towns.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual parishes and township offices — not confirmed online.

### Newspaper Records
- **Key papers:** *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville, Schuylkill County, 1825–present); *Wilkes-Barre Times*; *Scranton Tribune*; *Hazleton Plain Speaker*; numerous patch-town weeklies.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, mine accident notices, coroner's inquest reports, Irish community news (parish events, AOH meetings), union news, Molly Maguires trial coverage.
- **Access:** Schuylkill County Historical Society holds the Miners' Journal archive; partial digital coverage on Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov); PA State Library holds microfilm of many coal-region papers.

### Immigration and Naturalization Records
- **Relevant ports:** Irish immigrants to the anthracite coalfields typically arrived via Philadelphia, New York (Castle Garden; Ellis Island after 1892), or Boston, then traveled inland by rail.
- **Passenger lists:** NARA; indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch for most of 1860–1900.
- **Naturalization:** See Court Records above. After September 1906, federal courts only. The Schuylkill County naturalization volume (1849–1915) is browse-only.
- **Irish immigrant organizations:** Ancient Order of Hibernians (AOH) chapters were active throughout the anthracite region; membership and benefit records may survive at local lodges or the AOH national archive.

### Tax Records
- **Pennsylvania triennial assessments (from 1853):** List householder, real estate value, occupation, nativity — powerful intercensal substitute. Not confirmed as a searchable online database; check county historical societies and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **FamilySearch external links for Schuylkill (1860–1900 window):** 2 curated links returned, both outside the target period (Tax and Exoneration Lists 1768–1801; 1850 Federal Census) — no curated external links fall within 1860–1900.

### Occupational / Mining Records
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855–1898):** ~41,000 colliery workers, occupation, wage rate, parish of origin. [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki]
- **Mine inspection reports:** Pennsylvania appointed state mine inspectors beginning 1870. Annual reports organized by colliery (not by person); record workforce counts by nationality. Physical copies at PA State Archives; some published.
- **Mine accident reports:** Coroner's inquests and mine inspector reports name victims and witnesses.
- **Company records:** Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Company records (dominant southern anthracite operator) at Hagley Museum and Library (Wilmington, DE).

### Mutual Aid and Fraternal Records
- **Ancient Order of Hibernians (AOH):** Active coal-region chapters; membership, benefit, and death records.
- **Workingmen's Benevolent Association (WBA):** Active 1868–1875; records may survive at local historical societies.
- **Molly Maguires trial records (Schuylkill County, 1875–1877):** Trial transcripts, Pinkerton detective reports, and court records name many Irish coal miners. Held at Schuylkill County courthouse; partially published.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 5 Schuylkill County volumes (Probate 1851–1930; Naturalization 1849–1915; Church 1842–1895; Deeds 1815–1900 [22% indexed]; Marriage 1870–1910); 3 PA-state volumes (Probate, Death, Naturalization [15% indexed]); PA Probate collection 1683–1994 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census 1860–1900 (indexed); Civil War service/pension records; passenger lists; partial Miners' Journal index | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records, pension files, Civil War draft registrations | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Partial digitization of coal-region newspapers | Free |
| FamilySearch — Specialized | Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index 1855–1898 (~41,000 colliery workers) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned all 5 Schuylkill County volumes (totalResults: 5 — complete set) and all 3 Pennsylvania state-level volumes (totalResults: 3 — complete set). County-level place standardization failed for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland, and Columbia — volume data for those five counties could not be obtained in this session and will require a direct FamilySearch catalog search by county name.

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville PA | County histories, Miners' Journal archive, genealogical files | In-person; limited remote |
| Luzerne County Historical Society, Wilkes-Barre PA | County and city histories, local records | In-person |
| Lackawanna County Historical Society, Scranton PA | City and county records, industrial history | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg PA | PA adjutant general records; county court records on microfilm; triennial assessment ledgers | In-person; some online |
| NARA Philadelphia | Federal court naturalizations; passenger lists; federal census originals | In-person; most indexed online |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives, Scranton PA | Catholic parish registers post-1868 | By appointment |
| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives, Harrisburg PA | Catholic parish registers pre-1868 | By appointment |
| Hagley Museum & Library, Wilmington DE | Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Company corporate records | In-person |

---

## Records NOT Online

- Pennsylvania triennial tax assessment ledgers (from 1853) — nativity and occupation listed; held at PA State Archives and county historical societies
- AOH (Ancient Order of Hibernians) chapter membership and benefit records
- Mine company payroll books beyond the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index subset
- Pennsylvania mine inspection annual reports (physical at PA State Archives; some published)
- Molly Maguires trial transcripts and Pinkerton reports in full
- County-level church registers not captured in the FamilySearch Schuylkill County Church Records volume
- GAR post records for coal-region posts
- Sexton records and burial registers for individual parishes and company cemeteries

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1890 U.S. Federal Census:** Largely destroyed by fire 1921. Triennial tax assessments and city/county directories are the best substitutes for that decade.
- **Company payroll books:** Most destroyed in the 1903 records consolidation. The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index preserves only the surviving fraction. [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki]
- **County-specific losses** for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland, and Columbia were not returned by the tools in this session — consult each county's historical society directly.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Search the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index first** for any ancestor in the lower anthracite field (1855–1898). Its ~41,000 entries include occupation and parish of origin, anchoring both an occupational and a Catholic parish research trail. [[Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)]

2. **Distinguish the two Catholic dioceses.** Pre-1868 → Diocese of Harrisburg. Post-1868 → Diocese of Scranton. Searching only Scranton misses all pre-1868 coal-region Catholic events. [[Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)]

3. **Triennial assessments fill census gaps.** Pennsylvania assessed residents every three years from 1853, with nativity and occupation — essential given the 1890 census destruction.

4. **Naturalization records before 1906 are scattered.** Check county Courts of Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, and federal district courts. The Schuylkill County Naturalization volume (1849–1915, 298 images) is browse-only.

5. **Deed Records are the most name-searchable FamilySearch holding** for Schuylkill County (22% indexed, image group 007936752, 1815–1900). Coal miners appear as grantees and witnesses.

6. **For Lackawanna County before its formation:** All records were filed under Luzerne County. Always search Luzerne County records for events in the Scranton area before Lackawanna was established.

7. **Payroll indexes vs. mine inspection reports:** Payroll indexes name individual workers; inspection reports are organized by colliery but show workforce composition by nationality. Use payroll indexes for personal identification; inspection reports for community context. [[Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)]

8. **Don't overlook the Miners' Journal (Pottsville, 1825–present).** Mine accident reports, obituaries, Irish community notices, and Molly Maguires trial coverage for the whole region. Schuylkill County Historical Society holds the archive; partial digitization on Newspapers.com and Chronicling America.

9. **The Schuylkill County Church Records volume is bilingual** (English and German, image group 007936751, 1842–1895). German immigrant neighbors may appear in the same registers as Irish parishioners.

10. **Columbia County** is not among the five counties named in the FamilySearch Coal Region Records wiki. Apply general Pennsylvania research strategies there unless you can confirm a coal-mining community within the anthracite field.

---

## Survey Gaps

The following FamilySearch resources returned generic (non-Pennsylvania-specific) content and should be visited directly on familysearch.org:
- All four `wiki_place_page` sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) for Pennsylvania
- Pennsylvania Vital Records; Pennsylvania Church Records; Pennsylvania Land and Property
- Luzerne County, Pennsylvania Genealogy; Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania Genealogy
- County-level `standardPlace` could not be resolved for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland, or Columbia — volume data for those five counties requires a direct FamilySearch catalog search by county name.

---

**Guide persisted** to your Patrick Flynn research project as `loc_001` — it will feed directly into any research plan you create next.

### What the FamilySearch wiki page on Pennsylvania Coal Region Records revealed

The specialized wiki page at [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) — the one you specifically asked to read — contains three findings that don't appear in any standard county-level guide:

| Finding | Why it matters for Irish ancestors |
|---|---|
| **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898 (~41,000 workers)** | Names individual colliery workers with *parish of origin* — can directly link an Irish miner to his home parish without a surviving passenger record |
| **Diocese split at 1868 (Harrisburg → Scranton)** | Pre-1868 Catholic baptisms/marriages are at Harrisburg, not Scranton — a gap most researchers never check |
| **Triennial state assessments from 1853 include nativity** | Fills the 1890 census void and confirms Irish origin for workers who appear nowhere else |

7. **Payroll indexes vs. inspection reports:** Payroll indexes name individual workers; mine inspection reports are organized by colliery but show workforce composition by nationality. ### Mutual Aid and Fraternal Records
- **Ancient Order of Hibernians (AOH):** Irish Catholic fraternal organization with active coal-region chapters; membership, benefit, and death records.
- **Workingmen's Benevolent Association (WBA):** Active 1868–1875; union records may survive at local historical societies.
- **Molly Maguires trial records (Schuylkill County, 1875–1877):** Trial transcripts, Pinkerton detective reports, and court records name many Irish coal miners; held at Schuylkill County courthouse, partially published.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |

| FamilySearch | 5 Schuylkill County volumes (Probate 1851–1930; Naturalization 1849–1915; Church 1842–1895; Deeds 1815–1900 [22% indexed]; Marriage 1870–1910); 3 PA-state volumes (Probate, Death, Naturalization [15% indexed]); PA Probate collection 1683–1994 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census 1860–1900 (indexed); Civil War service/pension records; passenger lists; partial Miners' Journal index | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records, pension files, Civil War draft registrations | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Partial digitization of coal-region newspapers | Free |
| FamilySearch — Specialized | Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index 1855–1898 (~41,000 colliery workers) | Free |

| Lackawanna County Historical Society, Scranton PA | City and county records, industrial history | In-person |

## Records NOT Online

- Pennsylvania triennial tax assessment ledgers (from 1853) — nativity and occupation listed; held at PA State Archives and county historical societies; not confirmed as searchable online
- AOH (Ancient Order of Hibernians) chapter membership and benefit records
- Mine company payroll books beyond the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index subset
- Pennsylvania mine inspection annual reports (physical at PA State Archives; some published in print)
- Molly Maguires trial transcripts and Pinkerton reports in full
- County-level church registers not captured in the FamilySearch Schuylkill Church Records volume
- GAR post records for coal-region posts
- Sexton records and burial registers for individual parishes and company cemeteries

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1890 U.S. Federal Census:** Largely destroyed by fire 1921. Triennial tax assessments and city/county directories are the best substitutes for that decade.
- **Company payroll books:** Most destroyed in the 1903 records consolidation. The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index preserves only the fraction of payroll books that survived. [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki]
- **County-specific losses** for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland, and Columbia were not returned by the tools in this session. Consult each county's historical society for courthouse fire or flood losses.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Search the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index first** for any ancestor in the lower anthracite field (1855–1898). Its ~41,000 entries include occupation and parish of origin, which anchor both an occupational and a Catholic parish research trail. [[Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)]

2. **Distinguish the two dioceses.** Catholic baptisms/marriages/burials before 1868 → Diocese of Harrisburg. After 1868 → Diocese of Scranton. Many researchers search only Scranton and miss all pre-1868 events. [[Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)]

3. **Triennial assessments fill census gaps.** Pennsylvania assessed residents every three years from 1853 with nativity and occupation — essential given the 1890 federal census destruction.

4. **Naturalization records before 1906 are scattered.** Check county Courts of Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, and federal district courts. The Schuylkill County Naturalization volume (1849–1915, 298 images) is browse-only — budget time to page through it.

5. **Deed Records are the most searchable FamilySearch land record** for Schuylkill County (22% indexed, image group 007936752, 1815–1900). Even renters and coal miners appear as grantees or witnesses.

6. **For Lackawanna County before its formation:** All records filed under Luzerne County. Always search Luzerne County records for events in the Scranton area before Lackawanna was established.

7. **Payroll indexes vs. inspection reports:** Payroll indexes name individual workers; mine inspection reports are organized by colliery but show workforce composition by nationality. Use payroll indexes for personal identification; inspection reports for community context. [[Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)]

8. **Don't overlook the Miners' Journal (Pottsville, 1825–present).** It published mine accident reports, obituaries, Irish community notices, and Molly Maguires trial coverage for the entire region. Schuylkill County Historical Society holds the archive; partial digitization on Newspapers.com and Chronicling America.

9. **The Schuylkill County Church Records volume is bilingual** (English and German, image group 007936751, 1842–1895). German immigrant neighbors may appear in the same registers as Irish parishioners.

10. **Columbia County** is not among the five counties named in the FamilySearch Coal Region Records wiki. If researching ancestors there, apply general Pennsylvania research strategies rather than anthracite-specific ones unless you can confirm a coal-mining community.

# Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide
**Target period: c. 1760–1791 | New Hampshire Grants → Republic of Vermont → Statehood**
*Grounded in FamilySearch wiki output at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy*

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Vermont's pre-statehood period involves three successive — and overlapping — political authorities. Records for the same family may be held in three different states' archives depending on which authority created them.

| Period | Jurisdiction | Record implications |
|---|---|---|
| 1749–1764 | **New Hampshire** — Gov. Benning Wentworth issued township grants ("New Hampshire Grants") | Land records held in NH archives |
| 1764–1777 | **New York Colony / State** — British Privy Council assigned the territory to NY; NY issued competing grants; settlers (the "Green Mountain Boys") resisted | NY colonial land records; NY's 1771 survey of NH grantees |
| 1777–1791 | **Republic of Vermont** — Vermont declared independence January 15, 1777; operated as an unrecognized republic for 14 years | Vermont's own land, probate, and governmental records begin here |
| March 4, 1791 | **Statehood** — Vermont admitted as the 14th state | FamilySearch's "Vermont, United States" jurisdiction starts here |

> ⚠️ **Critical quirk:** FamilySearch's standardPlace for Vermont carries `dateRange: +1791/` — the system does not recognize Vermont as a jurisdiction before statehood. Searching FamilySearch under "Vermont" will not surface pre-statehood records that are cataloged under New Hampshire, New York, or separately at the Vermont State Archives. You must search those parent jurisdictions directly for pre-1791 materials.

---

## 1. Land and Property Records ★ Prime Source for This Period

Land records are the richest and most reliable source class for 1760–1791 Vermont research, because the NH/NY land dispute generated exceptional documentation.

### The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule
The single most important pre-statehood record class named in the FamilySearch wiki:

> "The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule, prepared under New York colonial authority before statehood, enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry lists grantee, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This record predates any Vermont civil registration and is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state."
> — FamilySearch Wiki, *Vermont Genealogy* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)

If your ancestor was a land holder before 1791, this schedule is the first name-finding tool to reach for. It functions as a census substitute for the period.

### Other land record streams
- **New Hampshire grant records (1749–1764):** Wentworth-era township grants; held in New Hampshire State Archives
- **New York competing grants (1764–1777):** New York State Archives holds NY colonial land papers for this territory
- **Republic of Vermont town proprietors' records (1777–1791):** Early deeds and proprietors' votes created under the Republic; held at individual town clerk offices and the Vermont State Archives

### Town histories as land-record surrogates
The FamilySearch wiki specifically flags this access route:

> "Nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access."
> — FamilySearch Wiki, *Vermont Genealogy* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)

These are widely digitized on HathiTrust, Google Books, and Internet Archive. For pre-statehood Vermont research, a town history may be the only surviving transcript of proprietors' meeting minutes and land divisions.

**Digitization gap:** The FamilySearch wiki page `Vermont_Land_and_Property` returned only generic content — no Vermont-specific collection sizes, FamilySearch catalog IDs, or digitization levels were returned by this tool. Search the FamilySearch Catalog directly under **Vermont → Land and Property**.

---

## 2. Vital Records — No Civil Registration in This Period

**Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857** — per the FamilySearch wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). This is entirely outside the pre-statehood window.

**Town clerk records** are the civil vital record of choice for 1760–1791. The FamilySearch wiki notes that some town clerk records date back to the 1770s, but survival is **uneven**, and it directs researchers to consult individual town clerk offices directly. No statewide compiled series is referenced.

**The FamilySearch wiki page `Vermont_Vital_Records`** returned only generic content — no Vermont-specific registration dates at the town level, collection counts, or FamilySearch catalog references were returned by this tool.

### Substitute sources when town clerk records are absent

| Substitute | Access |
|---|---|
| Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | Denominational archives; FamilySearch Catalog |
| Family Bibles | Vermont Historical Society manuscript collections |
| Cemetery records / gravestone inscriptions | Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspaper vital notices | Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| Probate estate papers (name ages, relationships) | Vermont State Archives; FamilySearch Catalog |

---

## 3. Census Records — No Federal Census Before 1790

There is no federal census covering the pre-statehood period. The **1790 U.S. Federal Census** is the earliest population schedule and was conducted just months before Vermont's admission (census: August 1790; statehood: March 4, 1791). Vermont was included in the 1790 enumeration and it is the closest thing to a full-population snapshot for this period. Available on Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Census substitutes for 1760–1790
- **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** (land grantees — see §1)
- **Tax lists and rate bills** — held at town clerk offices and Vermont State Archives; often the most comprehensive resident lists between censuses
- **Military musters and Revolutionary War rolls**
- **Proprietors' lists** in town histories

---

## 4. Military Records

Vermont contributed significantly to the Revolutionary War (1775–1783), and the Republic of Vermont maintained its own militia through the 1780s.

| Record type | Repository | Online access |
|---|---|---|
| Revolutionary War service records | NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/); Ancestry |
| Revolutionary War pension files (M804) | NARA | Fold3; Ancestry; FamilySearch |
| Vermont militia rolls (Republic period) | Vermont State Archives; Vermont State Papers (published) | Partial digitization on HathiTrust |

**Digitization gap:** The FamilySearch wiki page `Vermont_Military_Records` returned only generic content — no Vermont-specific indexed collection details were returned by this tool.

---

## 5. Church Records

No Vermont-specific church records information was returned by the FamilySearch wiki tools — `Vermont_Church_Records` returned only generic content.

For the 1760–1791 window, church registers are the **primary vital-events source** since civil registration does not exist. Dominant denominations active in Vermont before statehood:
- **Congregational** — the dominant church in most early Vermont towns; records held by individual churches or the Vermont Conference of the United Church of Christ
- **Baptist** — active especially in eastern Vermont
- **Episcopal / Anglican** — limited presence pre-statehood
- **Quaker (Society of Friends)** — monthly meeting records, highly systematic

Search: Vermont Historical Society (Montpelier), FamilySearch Catalog ("Vermont — Church records"), and relevant denominational archives.

---

## 6. Probate Records

Vermont probate courts were established under the Republic of Vermont beginning in **1778**. Probate jurisdiction operated at the county/district level. Pre-1791 probate records are among the earliest formal legal records created by Vermont's own government.

**Digitization gap:** The FamilySearch wiki page `Vermont_Probate_Records` returned only generic content — no Vermont-specific probate district coverage, date ranges, or FamilySearch collection IDs were returned by this tool.

Search: Vermont State Archives; FamilySearch Catalog ("Vermont — Probate records"); individual county probate court offices.

---

## 7. Newspapers

Historical newspapers are cited as a FamilySearch-curated external resource for Vermont. Early Vermont newspapers (Vermont Gazette, Vermont Journal, and others) began publishing in the 1780s during the Republic period and carried vital notices, legal announcements, land sales, and runaway notices.

- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) — curated as an external resource
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress) — some early Vermont titles

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings relevant to 1760–1791 |
|---|---|
| **Vermont State Archives** (Montpelier, VT) | Republic of Vermont records; early land records; state papers; probate |
| **Vermont Historical Society** (Montpelier, VT) | Manuscripts; town histories; compiled genealogies; church records |
| **New Hampshire State Archives** (Concord, NH) | Wentworth-era township grants (New Hampshire Grants, 1749–1764) |
| **New York State Archives** (Albany, NY) | NY colonial land papers for Vermont territory (1764–1777); 1771 survey |
| **NARA** (https://www.archives.gov/) | Revolutionary War service/pension records; 1790 federal census |
| **Town clerk offices** (individual VT towns) | Town vital records (some from 1770s); early deeds; tax lists |
| **FamilySearch Catalog** | Microfilmed collections — search under "Vermont" and specific county |
| **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) | Revolutionary War service records; pension files |
| **Ancestry.com** | 1790 federal census; compiled Vermont collections |
| **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records; gravestone transcriptions |
| **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical newspaper vital notices |

---

## Research Quirks — Know Before You Search

1. **FamilySearch's "Vermont" jurisdiction starts at 1791.** Pre-statehood records are cataloged under *New Hampshire*, *New York*, or the Vermont State Archives separately — not under a "Vermont" FamilySearch place. Adjust your search strategy accordingly.

2. **The same land parcel may carry two grants** — a New Hampshire grant *and* a New York grant covering the same acreage. Know which your ancestor held, and search both NH and NY archives for their documentation.

3. **The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** is the earliest systematic name list for the future state (per the FamilySearch wiki). For the c. 1760–1777 period, it is the primary substitute for a census.

4. **No statewide vital registration until 1857** (statewide level per FamilySearch wiki). Town clerk records — where they survive — are the civil records of choice. Absence of a town clerk entry does not mean the event did not occur; the register may simply not survive.

5. **Town histories are a primary-access route, not just background reading.** Colonial-era proprietors' records reprinted in 19th-century town histories may be the only surviving transcription of those records (FamilySearch wiki). Find them on HathiTrust, Google Books, and Internet Archive.

6. **The 1790 federal census** is technically post-statehood (Vermont admitted March 4, 1791; census taken August 1790), but it is the closest systematic full-population record for families in this study period. It is also the *earliest* federal census covering Vermont.

7. **Republic of Vermont records (1777–1791)** are a distinct body — Vermont's own government created land, probate, court, and militia records during its 14 years as an independent republic, before any U.S. federal jurisdiction applied. The Vermont State Archives is the primary custodian.
